Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, 14(2), 1590–1606, 2023
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3200704
Main topics: distribution locational marginal pricing (DLMP); uncertainty pricing; uncertainty DLMP; transmission-distribution coordination; wholesale electricity market; robust optimization; distributed energy resources (DERs); reserve; heterogeneous decomposition (HGD); voltage; congestion; network loss

Quick takeaway

This paper develops an uncertainty-aware DLMP mechanism for a day-ahead distribution electricity market and explicitly coordinates it with the transmission-level wholesale market.

The central question is:

How can a distribution market simultaneously price active power, reactive power, and renewable uncertainty while keeping its market-clearing results and price signals consistent with the wholesale electricity market?

The proposed framework introduces three distribution-level prices:

  • active-power DLMP for active energy;
  • reactive-power DLMP for reactive energy;
  • uncertainty DLMP for uncertainty and reserve.

The uncertainty DLMP charges renewable DERs for forecast uncertainty and rewards resources that provide reserve to mitigate that uncertainty. Meanwhile, a decentralized heterogeneous decomposition (HGD) algorithm coordinates TSO and DSOs by iteratively exchanging only boundary power/reserve quantities and boundary prices.

The main conceptual contribution is therefore not just a new DLMP formula. It is a unified pricing architecture linking:

wholesale LMP/ULMP → TSO–DSO coordination → distribution DLMPs → DER energy/reserve/uncertainty settlement.

1. Problem addressed

Distribution systems are increasingly populated by small-scale DERs such as:

  • PV;
  • wind turbines;
  • microturbines;
  • energy storage systems.

A local distribution electricity market can coordinate these resources, but two problems become increasingly important.

Renewable uncertainty

PV and wind forecast errors can create:

  • overvoltage;
  • congestion;
  • extra reserve requirements;
  • additional operating cost.

A conventional deterministic DLMP does not directly assign an economic responsibility to the uncertainty source.

Transmission-distribution interaction

Distribution systems are not isolated from the wholesale market.

Large-scale DER scheduling changes the net demand seen by the transmission system. This changes:

  • transmission dispatch;
  • LMPs;
  • reserve requirements.

In turn, transmission-level LMPs influence:

  • DSO purchases from the TSO;
  • local DER scheduling;
  • local DLMP formation.

The paper therefore treats uncertainty pricing and TSO–DSO market coordination as one integrated problem.

2. Why ordinary DLMP is insufficient under uncertainty

Conventional DLMP methods generally price the marginal cost of serving additional demand at a distribution node.

They can reflect:

  • energy cost;
  • network loss;
  • congestion;
  • voltage constraints.

However, if renewable forecast uncertainty is ignored, two market participants with the same expected energy injection can receive the same energy-related price signal even if one creates much larger balancing requirements.

This produces a missing economic signal:

who creates uncertainty, and who provides the flexibility required to absorb it?

The paper therefore introduces an explicit uncertainty price at each distribution node.

3. Why transmission-distribution coordination is necessary

A common simplification in DLMP studies is to assume that the LMP at the substation is fixed.

The paper argues that this can be problematic when distribution-level DER penetration becomes large.

If DSOs and the TSO clear independently:

  • system-wide generation resources may not be fully utilized;
  • congestion may become more serious;
  • wholesale prices may be distorted;
  • boundary power mismatches may occur;
  • the distribution market may respond to an LMP that would itself change if the DSO changed its demand.

So the boundary price should be endogenous to the interaction rather than treated as an external constant.

4. Transmission-distribution coordinated market framework

The framework contains one TSO and multiple DSOs.

Transmission level

The TSO clears a robust wholesale market involving:

  • thermal generators;
  • wind farms;
  • load-serving entities;
  • distribution systems.

The TSO determines:

  • energy dispatch;
  • reserve dispatch;
  • LMP for active energy;
  • ULMP for uncertainty/reserve.

Distribution level

Each DSO clears its local distribution market involving:

  • renewable DERs;
  • microturbines;
  • ESSs;
  • loads;
  • the upstream transmission system.

Each DSO determines:

  • local active/reactive DER schedules;
  • local reserve;
  • active-power DLMP;
  • reactive-power DLMP;
  • uncertainty DLMP;
  • active-energy and reserve demand from the TSO.

The two levels iterate until boundary quantities converge.

5. What is ULMP at the transmission level?

The wholesale market has two related marginal prices.

LMP

The transmission LMP prices the marginal cost of serving an additional unit of forecast net load.

Its formulation contains:

  • system energy component;
  • transmission congestion component.

ULMP

The uncertainty locational marginal price (ULMP) prices the marginal cost of an additional unit of net-load forecast deviation.

It therefore reflects the marginal value of reserve and the network impact of uncertainty.

Conceptually:

LMP → energy
ULMP → uncertainty / reserve

The DSO receives both signals at the transmission-distribution boundary.

6. Robust wholesale-market clearing

The transmission market minimizes:

  1. thermal generation energy cost; and
  2. reserve cost.

The model contains two coupled operating states.

Dispatch state

Schedules generation to meet the forecast net load.

Redispatch state

Deploys reserve to cope with worst-case forecast deviations.

The transmission uncertainty set is modeled as a box set for:

  • load forecast errors;
  • wind forecast errors.

The robust model therefore seeks a schedule that remains feasible for the specified uncertainty bounds.

7. Why robust optimization is used

The authors compare robust optimization conceptually with stochastic and chance-constrained methods.

The main reasons given for using robust optimization are:

  • it does not require a probability distribution for uncertain variables;
  • it has lower data requirements;
  • it avoids very large scenario sets;
  • it produces a solution against the worst case within the uncertainty set;
  • this is consistent with risk-averse power-system operation.

The trade-off is that the result depends strongly on how the uncertainty set is selected.

8. Distribution-level robust scheduling model

At the distribution level, the DSO first solves a robust scheduling model.

The model jointly determines the cost of:

  • purchasing active energy from the transmission system;
  • purchasing reactive energy from the transmission system;
  • purchasing reserve from the transmission system;
  • scheduling local DER active/reactive power;
  • scheduling local microturbine reserve.

The distribution network is represented using a branch-flow formulation with second-order-cone constraints so that important distribution-system characteristics are retained.

These include:

  • active and reactive power flow;
  • voltage magnitude;
  • line-current limits;
  • network losses;
  • line-capacity limits.

9. DER models represented in the DSO problem

The distribution market includes three main DER categories.

Renewable DERs

PV and wind have:

  • forecast active power;
  • bounded forecast error;
  • reactive-power capability constrained by minimum power factor.

Microturbines

Microturbines provide:

  • active energy;
  • reactive power;
  • upward reserve.

Their operation is constrained by:

  • apparent-power capacity;
  • ramping limits.

Energy storage systems

ESSs provide:

  • charging/discharging active power;
  • reactive power through the inverter.

The model includes:

  • charging/discharging efficiency;
  • SOC bounds;
  • terminal-energy constraint;
  • inverter capacity.

10. Why the paper uses a second model for DLMP derivation

The robust branch-flow scheduling problem is convex and could theoretically provide dual prices.

However, the authors argue that such convex-price expressions are not sufficiently intuitive for market interpretation and settlement.

Therefore, they use a two-step approach:

  1. solve the detailed robust scheduling model to obtain the worst-case realization and operating point;
  2. construct a linear programming market-clearing model around that operating point.

This makes the price components easier to decompose and interpret.

11. Linearized power-flow ingredients

Three main techniques are used.

Polygonal inner approximation

Quadratic apparent-power limits are approximated by linear inequalities.

Branch-flow and voltage sensitivity factors

The model uses sensitivity factors such as:

  • voltage sensitivity to active/reactive injection;
  • line-flow sensitivity to active/reactive injection.

Delivery factor and fictitious nodal demand

These are introduced to represent distribution network losses in the linearized model.

The delivery factor reflects how much of an incremental injection effectively reaches the network after considering losses.

The fictitious nodal demand allocates line losses to adjacent nodes.

12. Three distribution-level marginal prices

The paper derives three prices.

Active-power DLMP

a marginal price for active-energy demand.

Reactive-power DLMP

a marginal price for reactive-energy demand.

Uncertainty DLMP

a marginal price for forecast deviation / reserve requirement.

The uncertainty DLMP is the distinctive new pricing product in this paper.

It creates a direct settlement rule:

uncertainty source pays → reserve provider is rewarded.

13. DLMP decomposition

A major strength of the paper is that each DLMP can be decomposed into economically meaningful components.

For the active-power DLMP:

\[ \chi^p = \text{energy} + \text{voltage} + \text{congestion} + \text{loss}. \]

The reactive-power DLMP has an analogous decomposition.

The uncertainty DLMP also contains:

\[ \chi^u = \text{uncertainty energy/reserve component} + \text{voltage} + \text{congestion} + \text{loss}. \]

This decomposition allows the DSO to explain why two nodes receive different prices.

14. Why active and reactive DLMPs also change with uncertainty

An important result is that uncertainty does not only affect the newly introduced uncertainty DLMP.

The active and reactive DLMPs also include dual variables associated with the redispatch state.

Therefore uncertainty can change:

  • voltage scarcity;
  • line congestion;
  • reserve deployment;
  • marginal losses.

As a result:

more renewable uncertainty can increase active-power DLMP, reactive-power DLMP, and uncertainty DLMP simultaneously.

This is important because energy and reserve are co-optimized rather than treated as independent products.

15. Settlement rule for DERs

A distribution-level participant can have four relevant quantities:

  • active power generation;
  • reactive power generation;
  • reserve provision;
  • uncertainty contribution.

The participant revenue is represented conceptually as:

\[ \text{Revenue} = \chi^p P + \chi^q Q + \chi^u R - \chi^u U. \]

So:

  • active generation earns active-power DLMP;
  • reactive generation earns reactive-power DLMP;
  • reserve earns uncertainty DLMP;
  • forecast uncertainty is charged at uncertainty DLMP.

This gives uncertainty an explicit market price rather than treating it as a system-wide externality.

16. The uncertainty price can be negative in one component

A particularly interesting result appears in the voltage component of the uncertainty DLMP.

One might expect reserve always to be rewarded.

However, the paper shows cases in which the voltage component is negative.

The reason is physical:

  • reserve is scheduled to respond to renewable uncertainty;
  • if fully deployed, additional active generation may aggravate an existing overvoltage problem;
  • therefore additional reserve at that location can have a negative marginal value for voltage management.

So the price signal tells the microturbine to reduce reserve, even though reserve is normally considered beneficial.

This demonstrates why a locational uncertainty price contains more information than a system-wide reserve price.

17. Wholesale LMP and ULMP results

The case study shows that wholesale LMPs and ULMPs vary by transmission bus when network congestion occurs.

The paper reports spatial price differences particularly in:

  • hours 1–2;
  • hour 8;
  • hours 17–24.

Bus D generally has the highest wholesale price, followed by bus C.

This is important because the distribution systems connected to buses C and D inherit different boundary price signals.

Therefore two otherwise identical distribution networks can obtain different DLMPs purely because they are connected to different transmission locations.

18. Distribution DLMPs follow the boundary price but are not identical to it

The active-power DLMPs in each distribution system are strongly correlated with the boundary LMP.

Similarly, uncertainty DLMPs are strongly correlated with the boundary ULMP.

The transmission system can be viewed from the DSO perspective as a virtual marginal source.

When the DSO imports marginal energy or reserve from the TSO:

  • boundary LMP determines the energy component of active-power DLMP;
  • boundary ULMP determines the energy component of uncertainty DLMP.

However, local distribution prices are not simply copies of the transmission prices.

They are modified by local:

  • voltage;
  • congestion;
  • loss conditions.

19. Important exception: the boundary ULMP does not always determine the uncertainty-DLMP energy component

During hours 1–7 and 9–10 in the reported case, the distribution systems at buses C and D do not exchange reserve with the TSO.

Local microturbines provide the required reserve instead.

In those hours, the marginal reserve provider is local rather than upstream.

Therefore:

boundary ULMP ≠ uncertainty-DLMP energy component.

This is a useful market interpretation:

the marginal resource, not simply the physical interconnection, determines the marginal price component.

20. Uncertainty DLMP results

The uncertainty DLMP varies:

  • over time;
  • between distribution systems;
  • among nodes within the same distribution system.

The dominant variation is driven by the upstream ULMP / marginal reserve cost.

Smaller nodal differences are created by:

  • voltage constraints;
  • local congestion;
  • network losses.

This is exactly the feature the authors want from uncertainty pricing:

uncertainty should be priced according to both when and where it stresses the system.

21. Voltage component: example at node 18

For node 18 at hour 7, the paper reports an active-power-DLMP voltage component of:

−2.45 $/MWh

with decomposition:

  • dispatch part: −0.36 $/MWh;
  • redispatch part: −2.09 $/MWh.

The negative value corresponds to binding upper-voltage constraints.

The economic signal therefore encourages microturbines and ESSs to reduce active-power generation so that overvoltage is alleviated.

The larger redispatch component also shows that uncertainty is responsible for most of the marginal voltage problem in that example.

22. Congestion component: reverse-flow and uncertainty effects

The paper gives two illustrative cases.

Hour 11 — dispatch congestion

Large PV production creates reverse active-power flow and congestion on line (2,3).

The congestion component becomes negative for many nodes.

The resulting DLMP signal encourages controllable DERs to reduce active generation.

Hour 6 — redispatch congestion

Wind uncertainty creates congestion on line (1,2) during the redispatch state.

The price signal encourages DERs to increase local active generation/reserve so that the upstream line flow is reduced.

So congestion prices can point in opposite directions depending on the physical cause of the congestion.

23. Loss component

The loss component reflects the marginal effect of a nodal injection on distribution losses.

The reported price signal can be positive or negative depending on location and operating condition.

A positive marginal-loss component can reward DER generation when local injection reduces upstream transfer and losses.

Thus, even without congestion or voltage binding, nodal prices can differ because of losses.

24. DER scheduling responds to DLMPs

The paper demonstrates that microturbines choose between active energy and reserve according to local price signals.

When active-power DLMP is high:

microturbines prioritize active generation.

When active-power DLMP falls and reserve value is attractive:

residual capacity is used to provide reserve.

Two microturbines at different distribution nodes therefore obtain different dispatch even though they have similar technical parameters.

This is a direct consequence of locational marginal pricing.

25. Transmission prices change DSO purchases

The coordination also works in the opposite direction.

When boundary LMP and ULMP are high, the DSO tends to:

  • schedule more local DER active power;
  • schedule more local reserve;
  • purchase less active energy from the TSO;
  • purchase less reserve from the TSO.

When boundary prices are low, the DSO imports more from the upstream system.

This is the economic feedback loop that makes the transmission and distribution markets behave as an integrated market.

26. Sensitivity analysis: increasing renewable uncertainty

The renewable uncertainty bound is scaled by parameter \(\Lambda\).

The paper compares:

  • Case 1: \(\Lambda=1.0\);
  • Case 2: \(\Lambda=1.2\);
  • Case 3: \(\Lambda=1.4\).

For the distribution system connected to bus D, the reported average DLMPs increase as follows:

Average price Case 1 Case 2 Case 3
Active-power DLMP (\(/MWh) | 29.79 | 29.98 | 30.61 | | Reactive-power DLMP (\)/MVArh) 2.16 2.21 2.33
Uncertainty DLMP ($/MWh) 16.68 16.90 17.53

So uncertainty raises not only the uncertainty price but also energy-related marginal prices.

27. Uncertainty reallocates profit among market participants

As uncertainty increases:

Renewable DERs

Their reserve-related payment increases, reducing total profit.

For PVs in the bus-D distribution system, total reported profit decreases from approximately:

$304.51 → $247.88

across Cases 1 to 3.

Microturbines

Higher uncertainty creates more demand for controllable reserve.

Their reported profit increases from:

$786.60 → $826.01.

ESSs

Storage also benefits from greater flexibility value.

Its reported profit increases from:

$63.54 → $110.65.

The market therefore transfers value:

from uncertainty-causing resources → flexibility-providing resources.

28. Distribution uncertainty also changes the wholesale market

Higher renewable uncertainty in the distribution systems increases:

  • DSO active-energy demand from TSO;
  • DSO reserve demand from TSO;
  • distribution operating cost.

This in turn tightens transmission-level energy and reserve supply.

The reported average wholesale prices rise from Case 1 to Case 3:

  • LMP: 21.52 → 21.97 $/MWh;
  • ULMP: 12.88 → 13.35 $/MWh.

Transmission operation cost also increases.

This demonstrates why distribution uncertainty cannot be treated as purely local when DER penetration is large.

29. Heterogeneous decomposition (HGD)

The coordinated transmission-distribution optimization is not solved as one centralized problem in normal operation.

Instead, the HGD algorithm iterates between TSO and DSOs.

TSO sends

  • boundary LMP;
  • boundary ULMP.

DSO sends

  • boundary active-energy demand;
  • boundary reserve demand.

No full internal network model needs to be exchanged.

This preserves a degree of operational independence and limits information exchange.

30. Sensitivity terms accelerate convergence

The original HGD interaction can oscillate because:

  • the TSO price responds to DSO demand;
  • the DSO demand responds to TSO price.

The paper introduces:

  • sensitivity of LMP to boundary active-power demand;
  • sensitivity of ULMP to boundary reserve demand.

These sensitivities are estimated from previous iterations and embedded in the DSO objective.

They anticipate how the upstream price will move when the DSO changes its demand.

This is conceptually similar to giving the DSO a local approximation of the upstream system’s response.

31. HGD convergence and computation

Two systems are tested.

T5D33

  • 6 iterations;
  • 97.8 s;
  • HGD objective: 267451.01;
  • centralized objective: 267451.01.

T118D69

  • 10 iterations;
  • 857.5 s;
  • HGD objective: 2314927.58;
  • centralized objective: 2314927.58.

The identical objective values are used to verify the optimality of the decomposition method for the tested convex formulation.

The method is therefore intended for day-ahead market clearing rather than sub-second real-time control.

32. Main case-study structure

The primary T5D33 case contains:

  • a modified PJM 5-bus transmission system;
  • 100 identical IEEE 33-node distribution systems;
  • half connected to transmission bus C;
  • half connected to transmission bus D.

Each distribution system includes:

  • 8 PVs;
  • 2 wind turbines;
  • 2 microturbines;
  • 2 ESSs.

The ESS rating is 3 MW × 2 h per unit.

Distribution voltage limits are:

\[ 0.95 \le V \le 1.05 \text{ p.u.} \]

The test design intentionally shows that identical local distribution networks can experience different prices because their upstream transmission locations differ.

33. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — uncertainty should be a priced product, not only a technical constraint

Forecast error creates real operating cost and reserve requirements.

The uncertainty DLMP makes this cost visible to the source that creates it.

Lesson 2 — reserve should be locational in distribution systems

A MW of reserve can help one network constraint but worsen another.

Therefore a single system-wide reserve price may miss important voltage and congestion effects.

Lesson 3 — energy and uncertainty prices are coupled

Because dispatch and redispatch are co-optimized, larger uncertainty changes ordinary active/reactive DLMPs as well as the uncertainty DLMP.

Lesson 4 — DLMP should inherit information from the wholesale market

The distribution network does not have an independent marginal energy cost if it can trade with the upstream grid.

Boundary LMP/ULMP therefore naturally influence local DLMP components.

Lesson 5 — TSO–DSO coordination is a market-design problem, not only a power-flow problem

The quantities exchanged at the interface affect prices on both sides.

A coordinated market should therefore iterate over both physical quantities and marginal prices.

Lesson 6 — price decomposition improves interpretability

Separating energy, voltage, congestion, and loss components helps explain why a particular DER is rewarded or charged.

34. Limitations

Important limitations include:

  • renewable and load uncertainty are represented by bounded box sets rather than probability distributions;
  • robust optimization can be conservative if uncertainty bounds are too wide;
  • the framework assumes participants bid at marginal cost rather than behaving strategically;
  • reactive-power price at the transmission-distribution boundary is assumed constant because wholesale reactive-power pricing is not explicitly modeled;
  • the detailed distribution robust scheduling model is followed by a linearized model for price derivation, so the pricing formulation depends on the accuracy of the linearization around the obtained operating point;
  • the distribution systems used in the main case are replicated IEEE test systems rather than heterogeneous real feeders;
  • DER forecast-error correlations are not the main focus of the uncertainty set;
  • the market is day-ahead and does not explicitly model sequential intraday/real-time uncertainty updates;
  • the HGD method still requires iterative communication and several minutes for the larger test case;
  • reserve from microturbines is emphasized, while richer flexibility products from EVs, flexible loads, or aggregators are not modeled in detail.

35. Critical reading notes

Robustness depends on the uncertainty-set design

The uncertainty price is economically meaningful only relative to the uncertainty set used by the robust model.

If the bounds are too conservative, the model may over-procure reserve and overprice uncertainty.

If they are too narrow, the resulting schedule may not be sufficiently secure.

So a practical implementation would need a defensible method for calibrating uncertainty bounds from forecast-error data.

The transmission reactive-power interface is only partially coordinated

Active energy and reserve are iterated between TSO and DSO, but reactive-power demand is not sent to the TSO.

The root reactive-power price is treated as a constant.

Thus, the framework is strongly coordinated for active energy and uncertainty/reserve, but not fully unified for reactive-power market formation.

The market is not strategic

All participants are assumed to bid at marginal cost.

Therefore the paper studies efficient marginal pricing, not strategic bidding or market power.

If large DER aggregators can manipulate local prices, additional game-theoretic or equilibrium modeling would be required.

36. Research idea triggers

Possible extensions include:

  • distributionally robust DLMP using data-driven ambiguity sets rather than fixed box sets;
  • chance-constrained versus robust uncertainty DLMP comparison;
  • endogenous calibration of uncertainty sets from forecast performance;
  • joint active/reactive/uncertainty pricing with a fully coordinated transmission reactive-power market;
  • real-time or rolling-horizon TSO–DSO coordinated pricing;
  • strategic DER aggregator bidding under uncertainty DLMPs;
  • EV/V2G flexibility participation in uncertainty DLMP markets;
  • battery degradation-aware reserve pricing for ESSs;
  • prosumer flexibility and demand response under uncertainty DLMPs;
  • carbon-aware DLMP combining network marginal cost and carbon intensity;
  • green-certificate/carbon/energy/reserve co-pricing at distribution level;
  • privacy-preserving or federated TSO–DSO market coordination;
  • uncertainty DLMP for unbalanced three-phase distribution networks;
  • market settlement and revenue-adequacy analysis under uncertainty pricing;
  • learning-based prediction of nodal uncertainty marginal prices;
  • coupling uncertainty DLMP with VPP aggregation and bidding.

37. Position in the problem map

This paper can be placed in the following branch of an electricity-market literature map:

Distribution Electricity Market
│
├── Nodal pricing
│   ├── Active-power DLMP
│   ├── Reactive-power DLMP
│   └── Uncertainty DLMP
│
├── DER uncertainty
│   ├── Robust optimization
│   ├── Reserve requirement
│   └── Forecast-error charging
│
├── Network constraints
│   ├── Voltage
│   ├── Congestion
│   └── Loss
│
├── TSO–DSO coordination
│   ├── LMP / ULMP
│   ├── Boundary power
│   ├── Boundary reserve
│   └── Heterogeneous decomposition
│
└── DER settlement
    ├── Energy
    ├── Reactive power
    ├── Reserve
    └── Uncertainty

A concise summary is:

P023 extends DLMP from deterministic energy pricing to uncertainty-aware energy/reactive/reserve pricing and embeds the distribution market inside a coordinated TSO–DSO wholesale-market framework.

Problem-map tags: DLMP · uncertainty pricing · ULMP · robust optimization · TSO-DSO coordination · distribution market · reserve pricing · DER · HGD · voltage-congestion-loss decomposition

注记[P024] Wang et al. (2025) — EV scheduling with strategic siting, battery-aging compensation, and participation-aware dispatch

Citation / Paper information

  • Title: Electric Vehicle Scheduling Model With Strategic Siting and Incentive Pricing Considering Participation Willingness
  • Authors: Yanjia Wang, Da Xie, Chenghong Gu, Pengfei Zhao, and Xitian Wang
  • Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, Vol. 16, No. 6
  • Year: 2025 (November issue; published online 16 July 2025)
  • Pages: 5230–5245
  • DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2025.3589616
  • Main topic: Participation-aware VPP dispatch of EVs through charging-station siting, battery-aging compensation, charging-station-centered distributed scheduling, and iterative incentive pricing
  • Market level: VPP/grid-dispatch interface. The paper uses grid demand/generation conditions and incentive prices, but it does not formulate a standard wholesale market-clearing or bidding problem.
  • Main methods: three-step weighted K-means; DBI-based partition-number assessment; Gaussian-Copula Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis; battery-degradation-based compensation; station responsiveness ranking; distributed/sequential dispatch; dynamic occupancy pricing and distance-price redirection; iterative incentive price adjustment

Quick takeaway

This paper addresses a practical bottleneck in large-scale EV participation in VPP dispatch: even if EVs are technically available, owners may not respond because the dispatch requires additional travel, exposes the battery to degradation, or broadcasts requests to far more vehicles than are ultimately needed. The paper therefore treats participation willingness as a system-design variable, not merely an exogenous behavioral parameter.

Its main contribution is a coordinated chain of three mechanisms. First, charging-station locations are planned with a grid-state/SOC-aware weighted clustering method so that the EVs most useful to the grid are geographically closer to charging stations. Second, the dispatch incentive includes a battery-aging compensation term. Third, charging stations are ranked and activated sequentially so that fewer EVs need to be notified, thereby improving the response-realization rate and the modeled willingness to respond. The framework is validated with Chicago taxi-trip and charging-station data.

One-sentence takeaway: The paper improves EV willingness to participate in VPP dispatch by jointly reducing response travel, compensating battery wear, and replacing broadcast dispatch with charging-station-centered sequential scheduling.

1. Problem addressed

Existing problem

EVs are attractive VPP resources because they are numerous, mobile, and capable of both charging and discharging. However, the paper argues that existing EV scheduling studies mainly emphasize grid stability, charging cost, or aggregator/operator profit, while practical participation is constrained by EV owners’ willingness to respond.

Two willingness barriers are emphasized:

  1. Range anxiety: responding to a dispatch request may require additional travel to a charging/discharging point.
  2. Battery-aging anxiety: repeated charging/discharging can accelerate battery degradation, but conventional settlement may compensate only the delivered energy.

A third operational issue appears in large fleets: if a VPP broadcasts dispatch commands to all online EVs, the number of notified users can greatly exceed the number actually required. The resulting low response realization rate reduces the modeled willingness to participate.

Research gap

The paper identifies three gaps that are normally treated separately:

Charging-station siting
        +
Battery-aging compensation
        +
Participation-aware dispatch
        ↓
Need to be coordinated around EV willingness

Conventional charging-station planning mainly minimizes charging distance. This paper argues that VPP operation needs a different objective because the desirable EV type changes with grid condition: low/medium-SOC vehicles are useful for absorbing surplus generation, while high/medium-SOC vehicles are useful for discharging during shortages.

Similarly, conventional EV pricing often emphasizes operator economics, whereas this study explicitly adds compensation for battery aging from the EV-user perspective. Finally, it replaces fleet-wide broadcast dispatch with station-centered sequential scheduling.

Practical significance

The practical objective is not merely to make EVs technically schedulable. It is to make them more likely to accept and complete dispatch requests at a lower incentive price. In the case study, the combined strategy reduces travel distance, increases modeled willingness, and allows the 5.2 MWh response target to be achieved at a lower final incentive price than the baseline.

2. Overall framework

The paper’s architecture can be read as two data streams feeding three linked mechanisms.

Historical data
    ↓
EV locations + historical grid condition
    ↓
3-step weighted K-means
    ↓
Charging-station planning result

Real-time data
    ↓
Grid condition + EV information + regular electricity price
    ↓
Battery-aging compensation + station responsiveness ranking
    ↓
Sequential / distributed scheduling
    ↓
Complete VPP dispatch

The logic is:

Input → historical EV spatial/temporal data, historical grid generation/load data, real-time grid demand, EV SOC/location, charging-station availability, and reference electricity price.

Participants → grid/VPP dispatch side, VPP operator or dispatch center, EV users, dispatch-participating charging stations, and nearby non-dispatch charging stations used for redirection.

Market / optimization layer → this is not a conventional bid-clearing market. The paper instead constructs an incentive-and-dispatch mechanism: grid state determines which SOC group is useful; station siting is optimized accordingly; battery wear is monetized; charging stations are ranked; capacity is reserved; and the incentive price is increased iteratively if response is insufficient.

Information exchange → EV SOC and location are transmitted to the dispatch center; the paper assumes public cellular networks support real-time dispatch commands and response collection.

Output → charging-station locations, station dispatch order, selected dispatch stations, EV charging/discharging actions, redirection decisions for regular charging EVs, and the final incentive price required to satisfy the dispatch target.

3. Key models / mechanisms

3.1 Grid-state and SOC classification

The paper divides the power system into three operating states:

  • Power surplus: generation exceeds load.
  • Power shortage: generation is below load.
  • Power equilibrium: generation and load are balanced.

EVs are divided by SOC:

  • low SOC: 0% ≤ SOC < 40%
  • medium SOC: 40% ≤ SOC ≤ 60%
  • high SOC: 60% < SOC ≤ 100%

The core planning logic is not simply “all EVs should be close to a charger.” Instead:

Grid surplus
→ prioritize medium + low SOC EVs near stations
→ encourage charging / absorb surplus energy

Grid shortage
→ prioritize high + medium SOC EVs near stations
→ encourage discharging / support the grid

Grid equilibrium
→ conventional charging convenience dominates

A notable feature is the treatment of low-SOC EVs during shortage periods. The paper assigns them a negative clustering weight so that they are relatively farther from the planned station center, with the intention of discouraging charging when the grid is short of power. The authors describe this as flexible guidance rather than a mandatory restriction.

3.2 Three-step weighted K-means for charging-station siting

The siting method is designed for a very large EV data set and therefore decomposes clustering into three stages.

Step 1 — Clustering partition

All EV location samples are first partitioned geographically with K-means using Manhattan distance, motivated by the geometry of vehicle travel. The Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) is used to assess candidate values of the number of partitions.

Purpose:

  • reduce the number of points handled in subsequent weighted clustering;
  • preserve broad spatial structure;
  • make the later grid-state/SOC-specific clustering computationally tractable.

Input:

  • all EV location samples.

Output:

  • spatial partitions used independently in Step 2.

Step 2 — Grid-state/SOC weighted clustering

Within each partition, the paper applies a weighted distance:

d_{ij}=\beta_i\|x_i-\mu_j\|_1.

The weight β_i depends jointly on grid state and EV SOC. In the numerical implementation the effective values are 1, 0, or -1.

Interpretation:

  • β = 1: the sample attracts the cluster center;
  • β = 0: the sample does not influence the center;
  • β = -1: the formulation is intended to push the center away from that sample.

The updated center is a weighted mean of assigned samples. Thus the clustering is not merely identifying dense EV regions; it attempts to move station locations toward EVs that are useful for the current grid state.

Step 3 — Integrated clustering

The grid-surplus, grid-shortage, and grid-equilibrium layer results are merged. Each intermediate cluster center is weighted by the total weight/number of samples it represents, and a final weighted clustering produces the charging-station plan.

The final objective reported in the paper is a weighted sum of squared distances between intermediate centers and final centers.

Computational role

The paper reports approximate total time complexity as

O(N(KT1 + kT2))

after treating the Step-3 center set as relatively small. The point of the three-step structure is therefore as much computational decomposition as physical siting logic.

3.3 Uncertainty model for EV location, time, and SOC

The paper acknowledges that EV spatial location, appearance time, and SOC are uncertain and correlated. It therefore applies a Gaussian Copula-based Monte Carlo procedure to a four-dimensional data matrix containing:

longitude
latitude
charging / appearance time
SOC

The intended flow is:

observed EV data
↓
Z-score normalization
↓
empirical marginal transformation to pseudo-observations
↓
4-D Gaussian Copula for dependence
↓
Monte Carlo sampling
↓
synthetic EV behavior samples
↓
re-evaluate distance to nearest planned station

This is used as a post-planning robustness test rather than embedding uncertainty directly inside the siting optimization.

3.4 Priority adjustment for practical station retrofitting

Because a real city already has charging infrastructure, the paper introduces a priority index for deciding which proposed stations should be adjusted toward existing sites.

The priority combines:

  • the number of EVs around the proposed station;
  • the Manhattan distance to the nearest existing station;
  • a coefficient λ controlling how strongly adjustment distance matters.

The smaller the priority index, the higher the adjustment priority. This creates a practical “how much of the existing network should be modified?” layer on top of the ideal siting plan.

3.5 SOC estimation from taxi driving distance

The Chicago taxi data do not directly provide SOC. The paper therefore estimates SOC from cumulative passenger-carrying and empty-trip distance:

SOC at time t
= 1
- (energy consumption per km / battery capacity)
  × cumulative travelled distance before t

Purpose:

  • reconstruct a time-dependent SOC proxy from travel trajectories.

Important assumption:

  • SOC is inferred rather than observed; the paper does not explicitly model intermediate charging events inside this reconstruction equation.

3.6 Battery-aging compensation price

The paper defines the EV incentive price as:

incentive price
=
conventional dispatch price
+
battery-aging compensation

Battery aging is related to:

  • depth of discharge (DOD);
  • equivalent cycle life;
  • battery replacement cost;
  • dispatched energy relative to rated battery capacity.

The economic interpretation is straightforward: if a VPP asks an EV to discharge, the owner should receive a monetary amount representing the incremental battery-life loss caused by the dispatch.

The paper intentionally keeps this model simple so that the compensation mechanism can be transparent to EV users.

3.7 Response realization rate and willingness

Response realization rate is defined as:

RaR=\frac{\text{actual EVs dispatched}}{\text{EVs notified for scheduling}}.

The paper then uses a consumer-psychology response model from Ref. [43] to map RaR to willingness to respond.

Mechanism:

Notify too many EVs
↓
low realization rate
↓
low modeled willingness

Notify only the most responsive stations / EV groups
↓
higher realization rate
↓
higher modeled willingness

This is why the station-centered sequential scheduling strategy matters: it is not only a capacity-allocation algorithm; it is part of the behavioral model.

3.8 Charging-station responsiveness index

For each charging station, the paper calculates a responsiveness index RcI from:

  • number of high-, medium-, and low-SOC EVs around the station;
  • their average distance to the station;
  • SOC-specific weights;
  • a distance coefficient η_DAl.

During power shortage, high- and medium-SOC EVs increase a station’s ranking, while low-SOC EVs decrease it. During surplus, medium- and low-SOC EVs dominate.

Output:

  • a real-time ordering of charging stations from most to least suitable for dispatch.

3.9 Reserved capacity, occupancy control, and redirection

Each dispatch station reserves a fraction η_Sta of its allowable charging/discharging capacity for the VPP task. The remaining capacity can serve normal charging demand.

If regular charging consumes too much of the non-dispatch capacity, the charging price is dynamically increased. An EV that rejects the higher price, or arrives when no residual capacity remains, is redirected to another non-dispatch station by minimizing a weighted distance-price cost:

distance cost
+
charging-price cost

This mechanism separates two objectives:

protect dispatch capacity
        +
still accommodate ordinary charging demand

3.10 Flexible incentive-price adjustment

If the initial incentive price does not attract enough EV response, the price is increased by a fixed increment:

M(k+1) = M(k) + ΔM

until total response satisfies:

response energy ≥ dispatch demand + dispatch margin.

Thus the paper does not solve an equilibrium price analytically. It uses a feedback-like iterative price adjustment until the required response is secured.

4. Optimization problem

This paper is important to read correctly: it does not present one unified optimization problem with a single objective and one set of decision variables. It is a chain of coupled subproblems and decision rules.

Objective

The effective objectives are:

  1. Charging-station siting: reduce distance between dispatch-relevant EVs and stations under different grid/SOC states, while relatively discouraging unfavorable charging behavior during shortages.
  2. Final clustering: minimize a weighted center-to-center distance objective.
  3. Dispatch station selection: minimize the number of activated stations while satisfying required dispatch energy plus a margin.
  4. Regular-EV redirection: minimize a weighted distance-price cost.
  5. Flexible pricing: increase the incentive price until aggregate response meets the dispatch requirement.

There is no explicit system-wide objective such as “minimize total VPP cost” or “maximize social welfare” combining all five mechanisms.

Decision variables

Depending on the subproblem, the decisions include:

  • spatial cluster centers / proposed charging-station locations;
  • number of clusters allocated to each partition;
  • final integrated station centers;
  • priority for adapting proposed sites to existing infrastructure;
  • station dispatch order based on RcI;
  • number of stations N_All activated for the dispatch task;
  • available/reserved station capacity;
  • charging price for regular EVs at dispatch-participating stations;
  • redirection station j* for a regular EV;
  • iterative EV dispatch incentive price.

The paper does not formulate individual EV charging/discharging powers as one large optimization vector across a multi-period horizon.

Main constraints

The main constraints/mechanisms are:

  • SOC category definitions;
  • grid-state-specific weighting rules;
  • charging-station capacity reservation through η_Sta;
  • dispatch requirement:
sum of selected station capacities
≥ VPP dispatch demand + ε0
  • residual capacity available for ordinary charging;
  • redirection when residual capacity is non-positive or the EV rejects the dynamic price;
  • flexible incentive price iteration terminates only when response reaches demand plus margin.

Uncertainty treatment

The paper uses two different uncertainty treatments:

1. EV-behavior uncertainty

  • Gaussian Copula + Monte Carlo;
  • applied to location, time, and SOC;
  • 10,000 synthetic EV samples are generated for robustness evaluation.

2. Dispatch non-compliance / communication uncertainty

  • represented by a deterministic reserve margin ε0;
  • intended to cover communication failures and EV non-compliance;
  • ε0 should be calibrated using historical default rates.

The paper does not formulate a stochastic, robust, chance-constrained, or distributionally robust optimization problem for the complete dispatch process.

5. Market / pricing / game mechanism

Market type

The paper is best classified as a VPP incentive dispatch mechanism rather than a full electricity-market design paper.

It considers a VPP responding to grid demand and repeatedly refers to “electricity market demand,” but it does not model:

  • generator bids;
  • supply-demand market clearing;
  • LMP/DLMP formation;
  • reserve clearing;
  • auction equilibrium;
  • strategic bidding by the VPP.

Participant interaction

Grid condition / dispatch requirement
          ↓
         VPP
          ↓
select responsive charging stations
          ↓
EV users receive incentive signal
          ↓
accept / reject / charge / discharge
          ↓
aggregate response returned to VPP/grid

Incentive price formation

The initial price contains:

reference dispatch price
+
battery-aging compensation

If this is not enough, the price is raised by a fixed increment until aggregate response reaches the target.

Therefore, price is response-driven, not obtained from marginal system cost or a formal equilibrium.

Settlement

The paper states that battery-aging compensation is incorporated into the incentive price. It does not provide a detailed market settlement architecture among grid, VPP, charging station, and individual EV beyond this compensation logic.

Charging price for non-dispatch EVs

At dispatch-participating charging stations, ordinary charging users may face a dynamic surcharge when free capacity becomes scarce. This price is a congestion/resource-occupancy signal used to protect dispatch capacity, not the main VPP dispatch incentive price.

Game mechanism

No game-theoretic equilibrium is formulated. EV heterogeneity enters through the response model and iterative price adjustment rather than explicit strategic utility maximization.

6. Solution method

The solution architecture is algorithmic and sequential rather than based on MILP/NLP decomposition.

Why three-step clustering is needed

The Chicago data contain roughly four million samples. Directly applying weighted clustering to all points would be computationally heavy. Step 1 therefore compresses the problem spatially, Step 2 introduces grid/SOC preference within each partition, and Step 3 merges the partial solutions.

Large data set
↓
partition first
↓
weighted clustering within smaller regions
↓
merge cluster centers
↓
final station plan

Why distributed / station-centered scheduling is needed

A fleet-wide broadcast can notify far more EVs than needed. The paper instead aggregates information around charging stations, ranks station responsiveness, and activates only enough top-ranked stations to satisfy the response target.

This has two intended advantages:

  • lower communication/notification burden;
  • higher response-realization rate and hence higher modeled willingness.

Why iterative incentive pricing is needed

EV acceptance is heterogeneous and uncertain. A fixed price may not attract enough participants. Instead of predicting the exact willingness-price curve in one optimization step, the paper uses a simple repeated adjustment:

initial price
↓
predict / observe response
↓
insufficient?
   yes → add ΔM → repeat
   no  → stop

This is easy to implement, although it does not guarantee an economically optimal price in a formal market-design sense.

7. Case-study design

Test system and data

  • Geographic area: Chicago, USA
  • Mobility data: Chicago taxi-trip data, 2014–2022
  • Number of mobility samples used for siting: about 4 million sample points
  • Existing/planning station count used for comparison: 292 charging stations
  • Grid demand/generation data period: 2019–2022
  • Grid-state statistical source as stated by paper: PJM-related demand/generation analysis, cited to Ref. [45]
  • Software: MATLAB

Time representation

The paper divides a day into fixed historical grid-state windows:

Time Grid condition in case study
20:00–03:00 power surplus
06:00–08:00 power shortage
04:00–05:00 and 09:00–19:00 power equilibrium

The paper does not state a conventional optimization time resolution such as 5 min, 15 min, or 1 h for the entire dispatch formulation.

Clustering design

  • candidate Step-1 partition counts: 3–32;
  • DBI minimum occurs at 3 partitions: 0.5276;
  • selected partition count: 26, DBI 0.5579, because it substantially reduces subsequent computation while retaining similar clustering quality;
  • final number of charging-station centers: 292.

Weight matrix used in simulation

The implemented grid-state/SOC weights are effectively:

Power shortage:   high = 1, medium = 1, low = -1
Power equilibrium:high = 1, medium = 1, low = 1
Power surplus:    high = 0, medium = 1, low = 1

Uncertainty test

  • 10,000 synthetic EV samples generated;
  • variables include location, time, and SOC;
  • station-distance results are recalculated across scenarios.

Battery-aging / price parameters

  • battery example: 2018 EU version of BAIC Motor;
  • battery capacity: 45 kWh;
  • cycle life: about 1,200 charge/discharge cycles;
  • battery cost: about USD 3,184;
  • k_p = 1;
  • dispatched battery energy: 30 kWh;
  • paper reports compensation increment: 0.1474 added to the reference price.

Dispatch case

  • grid generation: 71,176 MWh;
  • grid electricity requirement: 71,297 MWh;
  • VPP dispatch task: 5 MWh;
  • dispatch margin: 200 kWh;
  • response target including margin: 5.2 MWh;
  • charging-station allowable energy parameter: P_e = 2 MWh;
  • station coefficient: η_Sta = 0.7;
  • dispatchable amount per selected station: 1.4 MWh;
  • required number of stations: 4;
  • responsiveness distance coefficient: η_DAl = 0.01;
  • average online EVs: 162,945 per hour;
  • flexible-price initial value: 1.1474 USD/kWh;
  • price increment: 0.20 USD/kWh per iteration.

Comparison cases

For charging-station planning, the proposed method is compared with:

  • existing Chicago charging stations;
  • planning based on station cost + user economic loss [17];
  • stochastic dynamic equilibrium planning [46];
  • flow capture location planning [47].

For dispatch pricing, the main comparison is:

Proposed
= optimized station layout + distributed/station-centered dispatch

Baseline
= original station layout + broadcast dispatch to all online EVs

8. Key quantitative results

8.1 Grid-state/SOC-specific clustering effect

The weighted clustering behaves as designed.

During power surplus:

  • medium-SOC distance to station: 0.0641 km
  • low-SOC distance: 0.0673 km
  • high-SOC distance: 2.413 km

During power shortage:

  • medium-SOC distance: 0.1070 km
  • high-SOC distance: 0.0991 km
  • low-SOC distance: 3.848 km

Thus, the clustering centers move toward the SOC groups that the VPP wants to schedule and away from the group whose behavior would worsen the current grid imbalance.

8.2 Final siting versus existing Chicago stations

The paper reports:

  • proposed plan: 95% of EVs can reach a station within about 0.8 km;
  • existing Chicago plan: about 2 km is required for 95% coverage;
  • proposed all-sample average nearest-station distance: 0.3155 km;
  • existing all-sample average: 0.5035 km;
  • reduction: 0.188 km, which is the value highlighted in the abstract and conclusion.

8.3 Comparison with alternative planning methods

Planning method Participation-scheduling distance (km) 95% radius (km)
Proposed 0.2995 0.7342
Existing Chicago stations 0.5413 2.1916
Cost + user economic loss [17] 0.3043 0.8643
Stochastic dynamic equilibrium [46] 0.3987 1.3115
Flow capture location [47] 0.3670 1.2856

Relative to the three alternative planning algorithms [17], [46], and [47], the paper reports participation-response distance reductions of:

  • 1.59%
  • 24.88%
  • 18.39%

respectively.

A subtle but important result is that during power shortage, the proposed method intentionally leaves low-SOC EVs relatively farther from charging stations than high-SOC EVs. The aim is not simply minimum travel for everyone, but state-dependent guidance compatible with grid needs.

8.4 95% coverage result

The paper separately states that under the proposed strategy, 95% of participating EVs are within 0.73 km, the smallest among the compared methods.

8.5 Uncertainty analysis

With 10,000 synthetic EV samples, the paper reports an overall mean nearest-station distance of:

  • 0.3262 km
  • 95% CI: 0.3165–0.3359 km

Scenario-specific mean distances in Table III range approximately from 0.2906 km to 0.3771 km. The authors therefore conclude that the siting performance is relatively insensitive to the tested uncertainty in EV location/time/SOC.

8.6 Practical retrofit workload

The paper finds that the largest growth rate of optimization benefit occurs when about 10% of stations are improved. Beyond 10%, the siting effect continues to improve but with lower marginal growth. The practical recommendation is therefore to prioritize the first 10% of station improvements.

8.7 Charging-station ranking in the dispatch example

The top four selected charging stations are:

Rank Station RcI
1 14 298.6425
2 114 93.1178
3 116 80.5819
4 118 74.2038

An interesting detail is that Station 114 ranks above Station 116 even though it has fewer high-SOC EVs (103 vs 129), because its high-SOC EVs are much closer on average (0.2667 km vs 0.4542 km) and it has fewer low-SOC EVs (1 vs 7). Thus the ranking is genuinely multi-factor rather than a simple EV-count ranking.

8.8 Dispatch-station occupancy control

The occupancy mechanism reduces regular charging usage at dispatch-participating stations. Examples:

Station Regular occupancy Dispatch-period occupancy
14 0.65 0.30
114 0.14 0.12
116 0.45 0.28
118 0.38 0.25

This is consistent with the setting η_Sta = 0.7, which reserves about 70% of the station capability for the dispatch task.

8.9 Schedulability versus alternative siting methods

For the top four selected stations, the sum of the responsiveness indices is:

Siting method Sum of top-4 RcI
Proposed 546.54
[17] 404.93
[45] as labeled in Table VI 389.79
[46] as labeled in Table VI 434.28

The paper interprets the higher total RcI as evidence that the proposed siting method creates charging-station locations with more favorable dispatchable EV composition and distance.

8.10 Participation willingness

The main willingness result is:

  • broadcast dispatch to all EVs: 0.0664
  • proposed distributed dispatch: 0.3907
  • absolute increase: 0.3243

This is one of the two headline numerical results in the abstract/conclusion.

8.11 Flexible incentive price

The dispatch target including margin is 5.2 MWh.

Iteration Price (USD/kWh) Proposed response (MWh) Baseline response (MWh)
0 1.1474 4.83 4.68
1 1.3474 5.04 4.92
2 1.5474 5.34 5.13
3 1.7474 — 5.37

The proposed strategy reaches the target at 1.5474 USD/kWh, whereas the baseline requires 1.7474 USD/kWh. Therefore, the proposed system meets the same response requirement at a final incentive price that is 0.20 USD/kWh lower.

The paper describes this as lower dispatch cost, although it does not explicitly calculate the total dollar dispatch expenditure for the two strategies.

9. What this paper teaches

1. Participation should be designed into the dispatch architecture

A useful conceptual shift is:

EV availability ≠ EV participation

A resource may be technically available but still unusable if owners dislike the travel distance, battery wear, or low realization rate of repeated dispatch invitations.

2. Infrastructure planning and operational dispatch should not be separated completely

The desired charging-station location depends on what the VPP will ask EVs to do later. This paper therefore makes siting dispatch-aware rather than treating station location as a static convenience problem.

3. “Minimum distance” is not always the right planning objective

During shortage periods, making low-SOC EVs extremely convenient to charge can conflict with grid needs. The paper therefore introduces differentiated spatial guidance by SOC and grid condition.

4. Compensation should reflect the asset cost borne by the participant

Battery degradation is not a system-side energy cost, but it matters directly to the EV owner. Converting degradation into a visible monetary compensation is a reusable idea for other flexible resources with wear costs, such as batteries, heat pumps, industrial equipment, or flexible electrolysers.

5. Dispatch selectivity can itself be an incentive mechanism

The paper improves willingness partly by not contacting everyone. More selective dispatch increases the response realization rate, which the behavioral model associates with higher willingness.

6. A simple adaptive price can be operationally useful even without a full equilibrium model

The iterative price update is conceptually simple:

not enough response
→ raise incentive
→ re-evaluate
→ stop when target is met

This can be attractive where exact participant utility functions are unavailable, although it sacrifices formal optimality.

10. Limitations

The following limitations are supported by the paper’s own formulation, assumptions, or stated future work.

1. SOC is reconstructed rather than measured

The taxi data do not contain SOC. SOC is inferred from cumulative distance using assumed energy consumption and rated battery capacity. The paper does not explicitly model observed charging events or direct battery telemetry in that reconstruction.

2. Taxi trajectories are used as a proxy for EV mobility

The case study is built on Chicago taxi trips. The paper uses these trajectories to represent EV spatial behavior, but no EV-specific revealed-preference data are reported for participation decisions.

3. Willingness is not directly calibrated from Chicago EV-user surveys

The willingness-response relationship is adopted from a consumer psychology model [43]. The paper does not report local survey estimation of the willingness curve for the Chicago case.

4. Battery aging is simplified

The degradation model focuses on DOD and equivalent cycle life and explicitly excludes some other sources of battery life loss, including the travel-to-station effect. Temperature, C-rate, calendar aging, SOH heterogeneity, and chemistry-specific electrochemical effects are not modeled.

5. Grid-state periods are historically classified rather than dynamically forecast

The case study assigns fixed time windows to surplus/shortage/equilibrium based on historical probability. A rolling real-time forecast of renewable generation, load, and market prices is not integrated with the siting/scheduling loop.

6. Dispatch uncertainty is handled mainly through a fixed margin

Communication failure and user non-compliance are represented by ε0. The authors explicitly identify more detailed robust scheduling under large-scale communication failures or extreme scenarios as future work.

7. No explicit network-constrained electricity-market clearing

The model does not include distribution power flow, voltage constraints, LMP/DLMP, feeder congestion, or a wholesale bid-clearing process. The “market” element is primarily the VPP incentive price and response mechanism.

8. No unified social-welfare or VPP-profit objective

Siting, station selection, redirection, degradation compensation, and price adjustment are linked sequentially. Their economic trade-offs are not optimized in one integrated objective.

9. Some algorithmic safeguards are not discussed

The weighted clustering permits negative weights. The paper does not describe what happens if the sum of weights in a cluster becomes zero or nearly zero when computing the weighted center.

11. Critical reading notes

Several reporting or mathematical points deserve attention. They should be recorded rather than silently corrected.

1. Equation (6): convergence-distance expression appears internally problematic

The paper prints the cluster-center change as a square root containing a difference between longitude and latitude increments rather than a standard nonnegative norm. Under a literal reading, the quantity can become negative inside the square root. This also differs from the Manhattan-distance formulation used elsewhere in Step 1.

Note: the present literature note does not “repair” the equation; the issue is preserved as reported.

2. Equation (7): DBI denominator uses a sum of cluster centers

The printed DBI expression uses a denominator of the form ||μ_i + μ_j||. Since the surrounding text describes separation between cluster centers, this is difficult to reconcile with the stated distance interpretation. A center-separation term would ordinarily depend on a difference, but the paper itself prints a plus sign.

3. Equations (30)–(32): marginal reconstruction after the Gaussian Copula is unclear

The method states that empirical distributions transform normalized variables into pseudo-observations and that a Gaussian Copula captures dependence. However, the final reconstruction is printed as a linear transformation x = uσ + μ. The paper does not show an inverse empirical-CDF step, so it is unclear how the original non-Gaussian marginals are restored.

4. Battery-aging compensation value in Eq. (54) is not transparently reproducible from Eqs. (39)–(40)

Using the paper’s stated parameters literally:

Mbattery = 3184 USD
Nbattery_DOD100 = 1200
Pdis = 30 kWh
Em = 45 kWh
kp = 1

Eq. (39) gives approximately:

(3184/1200) × (30/45)^2 ≈ 1.179

whereas Eq. (54) reports an increment of 0.1474 added to the electricity price. The paper does not show the additional normalization or unit conversion needed to reconcile these numbers. Because Eq. (40) directly adds the degradation term to a price, the unit basis of the compensation term should be clarified.

5. Data-source attribution around Ref. [45] is inconsistent

The case-study text describes 2019–2022 grid demand/generation data as being published by PJM and cites Ref. [45]. In the reference list, Ref. [45] is U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Open Data, not a PJM publication. This is a source-attribution inconsistency within the paper.

6. Table VI reference labels are difficult to reconcile with the preceding comparison description

Immediately before Table VI, the text states that the proposed method is compared with planning methods [17], [46], and [47]. However, Table VI labels the four columns as the paper, [17], [45], and [46]. This suggests a possible case/reference-label inconsistency.

7. Selected partition number is not the DBI optimum

This is not an error, but it is worth recording. The lowest DBI is reported at 3 partitions (0.5276), while 26 partitions (0.5579) are selected to reduce later computation more substantially. Thus the selected partition count is a computational trade-off, not the pure DBI optimum.

8. Abstract/conclusion headline values are internally consistent

The reported distance reduction 0.188 km matches 0.5035 - 0.3155, and the willingness improvement 0.3243 matches 0.3907 - 0.0664.

12. Research idea triggers

Participation model

Original paper
RaR → willingness via an adopted consumer-psychology curve

→ Possible extension
Survey-calibrated discrete-choice / latent-utility model with heterogeneity by trip purpose, income, SOC, urgency, and compensation level

Static siting

Original paper
Charging-station location optimized mainly from EV spatial data + grid-state/SOC weights

→ Possible extension
Joint siting-capacity planning with distribution-network constraints, feeder congestion, voltage, transformer loading, and charger investment cost

Historical grid-state windows

Original paper
Fixed surplus / shortage / equilibrium time blocks derived from historical probabilities

→ Possible extension
Rolling forecast or MPC using real-time renewable generation, load, price, traffic, and EV availability forecasts

Dispatch margin

Original paper
Fixed ε0 reserve for communication failure and user non-compliance

→ Possible extension
Chance-constrained / robust / Wasserstein-DRO dispatch calibrated from empirical response-default and communication-failure distributions

Battery-aging compensation

Original paper
Simple DOD/cycle-life compensation

→ Possible extension
SOH-, temperature-, C-rate-, chemistry-, and calendar-aging-aware marginal degradation price

Uniform iterative incentive

Original paper
One incentive price raised in fixed increments until response is sufficient

→ Possible extension
Personalized menu of contracts / mechanism design / inverse demand estimation with minimum-cost procurement of EV flexibility

VPP dispatch only

Original paper
VPP receives a dispatch task and recruits EV response

→ Possible extension
Day-ahead + real-time co-optimization of energy, reserve, regulation, and V2G bids with settlement and imbalance penalties

Energy-only participation signal

Original paper
Grid energy balance + EV flexibility

→ Possible extension
Energy + carbon + flexibility co-optimization, where the EV incentive reflects both grid balancing value and time-varying carbon intensity

Centralized data collection

Original paper
Real-time EV SOC/location sent to dispatch center

→ Possible extension
Privacy-preserving / federated station-level aggregation so the VPP can rank flexibility without receiving all individual mobility traces

Hand-designed clustering weights

Original paper
β ∈ {-1, 0, 1} selected from grid-state/SOC logic

→ Possible extension
Learn the attraction/repulsion weights from observed participation and dispatch success, while retaining physical constraints and interpretability

13. Connections to previous papers

Connection to P016 — demand-side market signals versus participation signals

P016 focused on a bi-level demand-side carbon market, where energy consumption, carbon responsibility, customized carbon prices, and user-to-user carbon trading form a market mechanism. P024 is different: it does not build a formal market-clearing architecture. Instead, it uses a VPP incentive signal to recruit EV flexibility.

The useful conceptual connection is:

P016
price signal changes demand because carbon responsibility is monetized

P024
price + travel + degradation + realization rate change flexibility participation

Together they suggest a broader research direction in which flexible demand/EVs respond not only to electricity price but to a stack of signals:

energy price
+
carbon price
+
asset degradation compensation
+
network / congestion value
+
participation convenience

P024 also complements market papers that optimize bidding or clearing: it addresses a lower-level question that those papers often abstract away — whether the physical EV fleet will actually show up and respond after the market has procured flexibility.
