注记[P025] Zhang et al. (2023) — Compact local-market representation via temporal-coupled feasible regions and umbrella constraints

Citation / Paper information

  • Title: Extracting Umbrella Constraint-Based Representation of Local Electricity Markets
  • Authors: Tiance Zhang, Jianxiao Wang, Qing Xia, Gengyin Li, and Ming Zhou
  • Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, Vol. 14, No. 2
  • Year: 2023 (March issue; published online 12 April 2022)
  • Pages: 1632–1641
  • DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3166793
  • Main topic: Compact representation of a local electricity market for coordination with the wholesale market by projecting detailed DER/network constraints onto a temporal-coupled feasible region (TCFR), then eliminating redundant constraints through umbrella constraint identification
  • Market level: Local electricity market ↔︎ wholesale market / ISO interface at the point of common coupling (PCC)
  • Main methods: polyhedral projection; duality; max–min feasibility diagnosis; LPCC-to-MILP reformulation; outer progressive approximation; dichotomy boundary search; umbrella constraint identification (UCI); parallel UCI (P-UCI); modified initial-space generation (M-ISG)

Quick takeaway

This paper asks a representation question rather than a conventional market-clearing question: how can a local electricity market containing many network constraints and temporally coupled DER constraints be submitted to the wholesale market as a small but equivalent model? Instead of exposing all internal line, voltage, PV, micro-turbine, and demand-response variables, the authors project the full local-market model onto the interactive power at the PCC. The resulting polytope is called the temporal-coupled feasible region (TCFR).

The central innovation is to combine two reductions. First, P-UCI removes non-effective internal constraints before projection. Second, outer progressive approximation constructs the boundary description of the TCFR, so the wholesale market only sees a compact set of equivalent constraints. In the modified IEEE 33-bus case, the original 12,882 constraints are reduced to 8,430 umbrella constraints and finally to a 192-constraint equivalent TCFR.

One-sentence takeaway: The paper converts a detailed, time-coupled local electricity market into a compact PCC-level polyhedral feasible region, then uses umbrella-constraint screening to make this projection computationally practical.

1. Problem addressed

Existing problem

A local electricity market can aggregate distributed energy resources (DERs) and demand-side resources so that the aggregate behaves, from the wholesale market’s perspective, like a controllable resource. The difficulty is that the aggregate is not naturally described by a few static parameters such as minimum output, maximum output, and ramp rate.

Its internal model may contain:

  • distribution-network power-flow constraints;
  • voltage and phase-angle limits;
  • PV output bounds;
  • micro-turbine (MT) capacity and ramping limits;
  • demand-response (DR) constraints;
  • coupling across multiple time periods.

If all of these internal constraints and variables are sent directly to the wholesale market, the information burden and computational burden become large, and private/internal information is exposed.

Research gap

Projection-based feasible-region methods had already been used for DER aggregation and TSO/DSO-type coordination, but the paper argues that complex temporal coupling is not adequately handled by existing aggregation methods. A local market with storage, DR, ramp-constrained generation, and other intertemporal resources creates a high-dimensional feasible set whose exact projection can contain many redundant inequalities.

The research gap can be summarized as:

Detailed local-market model
(network + DER + time coupling)
        ↓
Exact aggregate feasible region at PCC
        ↓
Need a compact, computationally tractable,
non-redundant representation

Practical significance

The desired interface is:

Local market / distribution utility
        ↓
submit a compact TCFR
        ↓
Wholesale market / ISO
        ↓
centralized economic dispatch
without seeing all local variables

The paper therefore treats model compression and exact feasibility preservation as the key enablers of local–wholesale market coordination.

2. Overall framework

The paper contrasts a conventional thermal plant with a local electricity market. A thermal unit can be represented by a small set of static parameters, whereas the local market contains time-varying DERs and internal network constraints. Its wholesale-facing representation is therefore the TCFR, not a simple capacity interval.

The workflow is:

Internal local-market data/model
(PV + MT + DR + network)
        ↓
Full constraint set ΦA
        ↓
P-UCI
remove redundant / non-umbrella constraints
        ↓
Projection onto PCC interactive power x
        ↓
Outer progressive approximation
        ↓
TCFR = {x | Dx ≤ d}
        ↓
Submit compact feasible-region model
        ↓
Wholesale market / ISO dispatch

Inputs

  • distribution-network topology and line parameters;
  • voltage/angle limits;
  • PV forecast/output bounds;
  • MT capacity and ramp-rate limits;
  • demand-response flexibility;
  • multi-period operating horizon.

Participants / institutional roles

  • DER users/resources: PV, MT, DR, and potentially other temporally coupled DERs;
  • local electricity market / aggregator / distribution utility: coordinates internal resources and constructs the aggregate feasible set;
  • PCC: physical and mathematical interface between local and upper-level system;
  • wholesale market / ISO: receives the compact TCFR and can treat the local market as one controllable participant.

Information exchange

The wholesale side does not need the detailed vector of internal variables y. It receives the feasible values of the aggregate interactive variable x, represented by linear inequalities.

Output

The final output is a compact polyhedral model:

R^{TC}=\{x\mid Dx\le d\},

which is intended to be equivalent, with respect to PCC exchange, to the much larger internal local-market model.

3. Key models / mechanisms

3.1 Full local electricity market model

The internal model contains three major groups of constraints:

ΦL : network / power-flow constraints
ΦD : DER capacity / static operating constraints
ΦT : temporal-coupled constraints

The paper then writes the full model compactly as

\Phi^A=\{x,y\mid Ax+By\le b\}.

Interpretation:

  • x: wholesale-facing representation variables, i.e. aggregate interactive power at the PCC;
  • y: all internal variables, including load, line-flow, voltage/angle, PV output, MT output, etc.;
  • A, B, b: compact matrices/vectors collecting the original constraints.

For a fixed aggregate exchange x, the admissible set of internal control strategies is

Y=\{y\mid By\le b-Ax\}.

Thus, an aggregate exchange is feasible only if at least one internal DER/network operating strategy exists.

3.2 Temporal-coupled feasible region (TCFR)

The paper defines TCFR as the set of all aggregate interactive powers x for which the internal feasible set is non-empty.

Conceptually:

High-dimensional local feasibility set
(x + all internal variables y)
        ↓ projection
PCC-level feasible set in x only
        ↓
TCFR

Mathematically:

R^{TC}=\mathrm{Pr}_x(\Phi^A)
      =\{x\mid \exists y: Ax+By\le b\}.

Because the original set is modeled as a polytope and projection is linear, the TCFR is also a bounded polytope and can be represented as

R^{TC}=\{x\mid Dx\le d\}.

The entire computational problem therefore becomes: find the correct boundary coefficients D and d.

3.3 Feasibility diagnostic model

For a candidate aggregate exchange x, the authors introduce positive slack variables and solve a minimum-slack problem. The diagnostic objective is the total forced adjustment required to satisfy the internal constraints.

Interpretation:

candidate x
↓
Can internal y satisfy all constraints?
↓
minimum slack = 0   → feasible
minimum slack > 0   → infeasible

This gives the basic diagnostic rule:

  • f(x)=0 → the internal feasible set Y is non-empty;
  • f(x)>0 → no feasible internal dispatch exists.

3.4 Worst-case infeasibility over the current candidate region

The algorithm maintains a current outer approximation R^C. Rather than checking one point at a time, it searches for the most infeasible point within this candidate region:

current region RC
↓
max over x ∈ RC
↓
min internal slack
↓
worst-case feasibility diagnosis

This yields a max–min problem. If the worst point is still feasible, then every point in the current region is feasible and the representation has converged.

3.5 Duality, LPCC, and MILP reformulation

The inner minimization is replaced by its dual linear program. This converts the max–min model into a formulation involving dual variables and complementarity conditions, referred to as a linear program with complementarity constraints (LPCC).

The complementarity condition is nonlinear, so the paper applies a big-M linearization, yielding a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that can be solved with CPLEX.

The important logic is:

max–min feasibility diagnosis
↓ dualize inner LP
LPCC
↓ big-M reformulation
MILP
↓
find worst infeasible point xO

The MILP is not a market-clearing MILP. It is a diagnostic/search problem used to construct the feasible-region boundary.

3.6 Outer progressive approximation

The outer approximation starts from a region that contains the true TCFR and progressively cuts away infeasible space.

The algorithm is:

1. Initialize a sufficiently large RC
        ↓
2. Solve MILP diagnostic problem
   → find worst-case point xO
        ↓
3. If xO is feasible
   → stop: RC is the TCFR
        ↓ otherwise
4. Connect known internal point xI to xO
        ↓
5. Dichotomy search
   → locate boundary point xB
        ↓
6. Use associated dual solution zB
   → generate a new boundary/cut
        ↓
7. Update RC and repeat

The method is “outer” because the current region initially over-estimates the true feasible region and is repeatedly reduced.

3.7 Boundary search by dichotomy

Once an internal feasible point xI and an external point xO are known, the line between them must cross the TCFR boundary. The boundary point is parameterized by a scalar λ and found through a one-dimensional root search.

Purpose:

  • avoid an expensive multidimensional search;
  • identify a point that lies on an active aggregate boundary;
  • recover the corresponding dual vector needed to form the new cut.

The authors identify the dichotomy step itself as a future target for acceleration.

3.8 Umbrella constraints

An umbrella constraint is an effective constraint that actually contributes to the feasible-set boundary. A non-umbrella constraint lies outside the active boundary and can be removed without changing the feasible region.

Geometrically:

constraint intersects feasible-set boundary
→ umbrella / effective

constraint stays away from feasible-set boundary
→ non-umbrella / redundant

The UCI formulation introduces a slack s_j for each candidate constraint:

  • s_j = 0 → constraint j is umbrella;
  • s_j > 0 → constraint j is non-umbrella.

The method therefore performs constraint screening before the expensive projection procedure.

3.9 Parallel umbrella constraint identification (P-UCI)

A direct UCI formulation becomes very large because it simultaneously creates variables/constraints for every candidate inequality. The paper observes that each constraint can be tested independently.

Hence:

one large UCI model
↓ decompose by constraint j
J independent LPs
↓ parallel solution
P-UCI

Each subproblem has approximately the same size as the original model rather than the multiplied size of the monolithic UCI formulation.

The purpose is not to change the feasible region. It is purely to remove redundant constraints and reduce the computational burden of later TCFR extraction.

3.10 Modified initial-space generation (M-ISG)

Theoretically, any sufficiently large outer space should work. The paper reports that solver accuracy makes the choice of initial space important in practice. If the initial box is too loose, some boundaries may not be correctly retrieved.

The proposed M-ISG therefore solves directional optimization problems around the full feasible set to construct a tighter initial polytope.

For a 2-D example, the search direction is rotated over N angular segments. The numerical illustration shows:

  • a very large generic boundary can miss two TCFR boundaries;
  • N=4 still misses some constraints;
  • N=8 retrieves almost all boundaries in the illustrated example.

Thus M-ISG is a numerical-accuracy aid rather than a separate market model.

3.11 Physical local-market constraints

The Appendix specifies the physical constraints used in the case studies:

  • linearized active/reactive line-flow equations;
  • piecewise-linear apparent-power line limit;
  • voltage-magnitude limits;
  • phase-angle limits;
  • PV output bounds;
  • MT capacity bounds;
  • MT intertemporal ramping constraints;
  • DR flexibility bounds and conservation constraint;
  • PCC active/reactive exchange equations;
  • nodal active/reactive power-balance equations.

A key modeling assumption is explicitly stated: the distribution power-flow model is linearized and line losses are neglected.

4. Optimization problem

This paper does not formulate one economic market-clearing objective such as social-welfare maximization. Instead, it solves several optimization problems whose purpose is to construct an equivalent feasible-region representation.

Objective

There are four main optimization objectives:

  1. Feasibility diagnosis: minimize total slack required for a given x.
  2. Worst-point search: maximize the minimum infeasibility over the current outer region.
  3. UCI/P-UCI: minimize a constraint-specific slack to test whether a physical inequality is effective.
  4. M-ISG: maximize support in selected directions to build a tighter initial region.

The high-level engineering objective is therefore:

preserve the exact aggregate feasibility of the local market while reducing the number of constraints and variables exchanged with the wholesale market.

Decision variables

Depending on the subproblem, the variables include:

  • aggregate interactive active/reactive power x at the PCC;
  • internal local-market operating variables y;
  • positive feasibility slack vectors;
  • dual variables z and v_d;
  • binary variables introduced by the big-M complementarity reformulation;
  • umbrella-test slack s_j and auxiliary vector w_j;
  • scalar line-search variable λ in boundary search.

Main constraints

At the physical layer:

  • network power-flow constraints;
  • voltage/angle bounds;
  • line apparent-power limits;
  • PV/MT output bounds;
  • MT ramping constraints;
  • DR flexibility/conservation constraints;
  • nodal and aggregate power balances.

At the feasible-region extraction layer:

  • dual-feasibility constraints;
  • big-M complementarity linearization;
  • current outer-region inequalities;
  • umbrella-constraint diagnostic inequalities;
  • line-segment relation between internal and external points.

Uncertainty treatment

The paper does not formulate stochastic optimization, robust optimization, chance constraints, CVaR, or distributionally robust optimization.

Time-varying PV and load profiles are included, but the case-study data are treated deterministically. The authors’ main focus is temporal coupling, not forecast uncertainty.

5. Market / pricing / game mechanism

Market type

The paper studies coordination between a local electricity market and a wholesale electricity market, with the local market represented as one aggregate resource at the PCC.

It is not a peer-to-peer trading paper and not a detailed bidding/game paper.

Bidding

No explicit strategic bidding model is formulated. The local market is assumed to submit its feasible operating region (TCFR) to the upper-level market.

Market clearing

The paper does not solve the final wholesale economic dispatch or clearing problem. Instead, it creates the representation that would allow the ISO to include the local market in such a problem.

The intended sequence is:

Local market computes TCFR
        ↓
TCFR submitted to ISO
        ↓
ISO treats local market as one resource
        ↓
wholesale dispatch can choose an x inside TCFR
        ↓
local market can recover an internal feasible y

Price formation / settlement

The paper does not specify LMP/DLMP formation, local clearing prices, settlement rules, or a payment allocation to DER users.

Incentives / participant interaction

The central mechanism is feasibility-information exchange, not price incentives. The local market gains privacy and lower coordination complexity because detailed internal constraints are not disclosed.

Game mechanism

No Nash, Stackelberg, cooperative-game, or bargaining formulation is used.

Participant optimization vs market clearing

This distinction is important:

  • Participant / local-market side: builds a feasible aggregate representation from internal constraints.
  • Wholesale market side: is assumed to use that representation later in economic dispatch.
  • This paper: focuses almost entirely on the first step and the interface representation.

6. Solution method

The need for the proposed solution method comes from the difficulty of exact projection with temporal coupling and many redundant constraints.

Why not simply enumerate vertices?

A direct enumeration method searches many directions in the aggregate space. As the number of DERs and the number of active boundaries increase, a large number of search directions is needed for good accuracy, causing computational growth.

Why outer progressive approximation?

It avoids traversing all possible directions. Instead it asks a targeted question:

"Is there any infeasible point left inside my current candidate region?"

If yes, the worst one is used to generate a new cut. If no, the current polytope is accepted as the TCFR.

Why P-UCI before projection?

Many original internal inequalities never become active. Keeping them increases the size of the repeated MILP diagnostic problems. P-UCI deletes these constraints without changing the feasible set.

The computational pipeline is therefore:

Original physical model
        ↓
P-UCI screening
        ↓
smaller equivalent internal model
        ↓
M-ISG initial region
        ↓
outer progressive approximation
        ↓
dichotomy boundary search
        ↓
compact TCFR

Solver / implementation

  • MATLAB R2016a;
  • Parallel Computing Toolbox;
  • IBM ILOG CPLEX 12.6;
  • reported hardware: 3.50 GHz, 128 GB RAM, Xeon Platinum 8160 CPU.

7. Case-study design

Case 1 — Modified IEEE 33-bus feeder

  • System: modified IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder
  • Horizon: 24 hours
  • Time resolution: 1 hour
  • DER types: PV, MT, DR
  • MTs: 5 units
  • MT installed capacity: 1 MW each
  • MT ramp rate: 0.2 MW/h
  • PVs: 7 units
  • PV installed capacity: 0.2 MW each
  • Local-market representation: interactive active/reactive power at PCC, with temporal coupling retained

The paper visualizes five single-period feasible regions at 03:00, 08:00, 13:00, 18:00, and 23:00, then uses three consecutive active-power periods (11:00–13:00) to visualize the time-coupled geometry.

Comparison methods

Three computational approaches are compared:

  • M1: enumeration method;
  • M2: proposed feasible-region characterization without P-UCI;
  • M3: proposed method with P-UCI.

M2 is also used to define the standard TCFR area for the error metric in the 2-D comparison.

DER-scale cases

Table I reports cases labeled:

  • 10 DERs;
  • 20 DERs;
  • 50 DERs.

The exact composition of these DER-count cases is not explicitly detailed in the reported case-study text.

Sensitivity study

DER installed capacity is varied from approximately:

  • 0.64 MW
  • up to 6.40 MW

in the sensitivity figure.

Case 2 — Caracas realistic distribution network

  • System: radial distribution network in the metropolitan area of Caracas, served by AES-Venezuela
  • Nodes: 141
  • Maximum active load: 11.90 MW
  • Maximum reactive load: 7.38 Mvar
  • PVs: 80

This larger system is used to test scalability of the three solution approaches.

8. Key quantitative results

8.1 Time dependence and temporal coupling

The single-period feasible regions change substantially over the day:

  • 03:00: small region due to low night load, weak DR capability, and zero PV;
  • 08:00: region expands as load and solar irradiance increase;
  • 13:00: largest region; reverse power flow appears and line limits alter the shape;
  • 18:00: active-power flexibility shrinks as PV output falls;
  • 23:00: feasible region becomes smaller again with low night load.

The main message is that a local market cannot be adequately represented by one static capacity interval.

8.2 Temporal-coupled feasible region

For active power at 11:00, 12:00, and 13:00, the TCFR is an irregular polyhedron rather than the cube that would arise if the three periods were independent.

The paper attributes this to intertemporal constraints such as:

  • MT ramping;
  • DR total-power conservation.

This figure is the clearest visual demonstration of why temporal coupling must be retained in the aggregate representation.

8.3 Constraint reduction — IEEE 33-bus case

The 24-hour 33-bus case contains:

Representation stage Number of constraints
Original local-market model 12,882
After P-UCI: umbrella constraints 8,430
Final equivalent TCFR 192

Derived reductions:

  • original → umbrella: 34.56% fewer constraints;
  • umbrella → final TCFR: 97.72% fewer constraints;
  • original → final TCFR: 98.51% fewer constraints.

The paper describes the first step as reducing calculation pressure by “about 40%” and emphasizes the much larger final reduction in information exchanged with the wholesale market.

8.4 Computational-time comparison — IEEE 33-bus cases

Case M1, 64 directions M1 error M2 time M3 time M3 time reduction vs M2
10 DERs 29.79 s 1.77% 6.60 s 3.37 s 48.94%
20 DERs 30.64 s 2.05% 8.04 s 3.48 s 56.72%
50 DERs 31.47 s 2.82% 11.79 s 5.33 s 54.79%

M1 is sensitive to the number of enumeration directions. For example, with only four directions, the reported errors are:

  • 10 DERs: 10.52%;
  • 20 DERs: 11.03%;
  • 50 DERs: 12.35%.

Increasing to 64 directions improves accuracy but substantially increases computation time.

The paper’s key computational point is that P-UCI approximately halves the runtime of the proposed characterization method in these cases without changing the represented feasible region.

8.5 DER-capacity sensitivity

As DER installed capacity increases, the TCFR expands.

The paper reports two regimes:

0.64–2.56 MW
→ feasible-region shape almost unchanged
→ many constraints are not yet binding

> 2.56 MW
→ feasible-region shape changes
→ additional constraints become active

At higher DER capacity, the upper-right expansion of the active/reactive power region is visibly limited. The authors infer that the limiting boundary is associated with a transmission-line safety constraint.

They also note an interpretability limitation: because an aggregate TCFR inequality is produced by projection of multiple physical constraints, it can be difficult to assign one exact physical meaning to a specific TCFR boundary.

8.6 Constraint reduction — Caracas case

The realistic Caracas model contains:

Representation stage Constraints
Original 57,938
Umbrella 35,096
Final equivalent 216

This shows that the compression mechanism remains strong at larger network scale.

8.7 Computational-time comparison — Caracas case

The reported values are:

Method Setting Time Error
M1 4 directions 21.87 s 11.32%
M1 16 directions 55.23 s 7.07%
M1 64 directions 190.23 s 1.98%
M2 proposed without P-UCI 104.08 s —
M3 proposed with P-UCI 54.92 s —

Relative to M2, P-UCI reduces time from 104.08 s to 54.92 s, a 47.23% time reduction.

Relative to M1 with 64 enumeration directions, M3 reduces runtime by 71.13%. The paper states that computational efficiency is improved by 246.4%; numerically, this corresponds to (190.23 - 54.92) / 54.92 × 100%, whereas a conventional “time reduction” calculation gives 71.13%.

9. What this paper teaches

1. Market coordination can be framed as an interface-model problem

Not every local–wholesale market paper needs to solve both markets simultaneously. A valuable research contribution can focus on the mathematical contract at the interface:

complex local system
↓
compact exact capability description
↓
upper-level market

2. Temporal coupling should survive aggregation

Aggregating each hour independently can overstate flexibility because ramping, storage/DR conservation, and other intertemporal constraints couple decisions across time.

A proper market-facing flexibility product may therefore need a multi-period feasible region, not separate hourly capacity bands.

3. Constraint screening can be as important as the projection algorithm

The paper’s major speed-up does not come from changing the final feasible set. It comes from recognizing that many detailed physical constraints never become active and can be screened out before repeated boundary-search optimization.

4. Dual variables provide geometric information

The dual solution is not used only for shadow prices. Here it helps construct a new aggregate-space inequality/cut. This is a reusable idea for flexibility-region and decomposition research.

5. Compact representation can support privacy

The ISO can receive an equivalent feasible-region model without receiving every individual DER variable or detailed local-network operating trajectory.

6. More DER capacity does not translate one-for-one into market flexibility

As DER capacity grows, network constraints eventually become binding and reshape the aggregate feasible region. Hence the market value of added DER capacity depends on internal network headroom, not only installed MW.

10. Limitations

1. Deterministic treatment of uncertain quantities

PV and load are time-varying but treated deterministically in the case studies. Forecast uncertainty is not embedded into the TCFR construction.

2. Linearized distribution-network model

The paper explicitly neglects line losses and uses a linearized power-flow model plus piecewise-linear line limits. The exactness of the TCFR is therefore with respect to the adopted linear model, not a full nonlinear AC distribution model.

3. Computational burden remains non-trivial

The method is significantly faster than the compared enumeration approach, but the Caracas case still requires tens of seconds, and the authors identify dichotomy-based boundary search as a remaining bottleneck.

4. No end-to-end market clearing or economic validation

The paper states that the TCFR can be submitted to ISO economic dispatch, but it does not quantify:

  • welfare effects;
  • clearing-price effects;
  • DER payments;
  • congestion rents;
  • profit allocation;
  • strategic bidding behavior.

5. Aggregate boundary interpretability is limited

The authors explicitly acknowledge that a particular TCFR boundary may result from projection of multiple physical constraints, so assigning one physical meaning to an aggregate inequality can be difficult.

6. Initial-region and numerical-tolerance sensitivity

The paper reports that an overly large initial region can cause some boundaries to be missed because of solver accuracy. M-ISG mitigates this, but this also shows that practical performance depends on numerical setup.

7. Big-M formulation requires numerical parameter selection

The LPCC is converted to MILP through a sufficiently large constant M. The paper does not provide a detailed sensitivity or systematic calibration procedure for M.

11. Critical reading notes

  1. “About 40%” constraint reduction is approximate rather than exact. The IEEE 33-bus case decreases from 12,882 to 8,430 constraints after P-UCI, which is a 34.56% numerical reduction. The text says the calculation pressure is reduced by “about 40%”; this should not be quoted as an exact 40% constraint-count reduction.

  2. The reported Caracas “246.4% computational efficiency improvement” uses a nonstandard denominator. M1 with 64 directions takes 190.23 s and M3 takes 54.92 s. The conventional runtime reduction is 71.13%, while 246.4% equals (190.23-54.92)/54.92. The paper’s statement is mathematically reproducible under that definition, but the metric should be explained when reused.

  3. Strict inequalities appear in the UCI equations. Eqs. (16) and (19) are written with <, while standard LP solvers handle non-strict inequalities. The paper does not explicitly state what numerical epsilon/tolerance is used to implement the strict inequality.

  4. The error benchmark uses M2 as the standard. The paper defines S^T as the TCFR area obtained by M2. Thus M1 is evaluated relative to M2 rather than against an independently derived exact analytical region. This is reasonable for the study but should be remembered when interpreting “accuracy.”

  5. The exact composition of the 10-DER, 20-DER, and 50-DER cases is not clearly specified in the case-study text. The runtime trend is clear, but reproducing those exact configurations would require additional implementation details.

  6. The paper uses “projection/project-based” wording inconsistently in prose. The mathematical development is clearly a projection-based feasible-region method; occasional “project-based” wording should be read in that sense.

  7. No major contradiction was found between the main conclusion and the reported numerical results. The results support the claims that P-UCI reduces problem size and runtime and that temporal coupling materially changes the aggregate feasible region.

注记[P026] Zhang et al. (2023) — Extracting Umbrella Constraint-Based Representation of Local Electricity Markets

Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, 14(2), 1632–1641
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3166793
Main topics: local–wholesale market coordination · distributed energy resource aggregation · Temporal-Coupled Feasible Region (TCFR) · projection-based representation · Umbrella Constraint Identification (UCI) · Parallel UCI (P-UCI) · network constraints · temporal coupling · computational scalability

Quick takeaway

This paper asks a very practical coordination question: how can a local electricity market containing many Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) tell the wholesale market what it can reliably deliver without sending the full internal distribution-network model? The difficulty is that the feasible exchange power at the Point of Common Coupling (PCC) is determined not only by network constraints, but also by intertemporal constraints such as Micro-Turbine (MT) ramping and Demand Response (DR) energy conservation.

The authors represent the whole local market by a Temporal-Coupled Feasible Region (TCFR). Any exchange trajectory inside this region can be supported by at least one feasible internal DER schedule. The TCFR is therefore an equivalent external description of the local market: the wholesale market can optimize over this condensed region instead of directly handling thousands of internal variables and constraints.

The main computational idea has two layers. First, Parallel Umbrella Constraint Identification (P-UCI) removes constraints that never form an effective boundary of the original feasible set. Second, an outer progressive approximation repeatedly finds infeasible exchange points and cuts them away until the remaining polytope represents the TCFR. In the modified IEEE 33-bus case, the original 24-hour model contains 12,882 constraints; P-UCI retains 8,430 umbrella constraints, and the final TCFR is represented by only 192 constraints.

The paper is especially useful as a study of physical feasibility abstraction. It is not mainly a pricing paper or a bidding-strategy paper. Its key contribution is to build a compact interface between a complex local distribution market and the wholesale market.

1. Problem addressed — how to expose local-market flexibility without exposing the whole local model

A local electricity market may contain photovoltaic (PV) units, micro-turbines, demand response and other time-varying resources. Internally, their operation is restricted by:

  • distribution-network power-flow and voltage constraints;
  • DER capacity and output limits;
  • intertemporal constraints, such as MT ramping;
  • demand-response constraints that couple decisions across time.

The upper-level wholesale market does not need every internal variable. What it needs to know is:

Which active/reactive power exchanges at the PCC are actually implementable by the local market?

A traditional generating unit can be summarized using relatively simple parameters such as minimum/maximum output and ramp rate. A local market is harder to summarize because many heterogeneous resources and network constraints jointly determine its operating flexibility.

If the local market sends too little information, the wholesale market may schedule an exchange that the distribution system cannot physically realize. If it sends the complete internal optimization model, coordination becomes computationally heavy and may reveal unnecessary internal information.

The paper therefore treats equivalent feasible-region extraction as the key interface problem between local and wholesale markets.

2. Why existing approaches are not enough

The paper divides existing coordination methods broadly into:

  1. Iteration-based methods, such as Lagrangian-relaxation-based coordination; and
  2. Projection-based methods, which project the high-dimensional local feasible set onto the variables exchanged with the wholesale market.

Projection-based methods are attractive because the local market can submit an equivalent model to the wholesale level and avoid repeated local–wholesale iterations during market coordination.

The remaining difficulty is temporal coupling. Existing feasible-region methods can become expensive when the original model contains many time-linked DER constraints. A local market with DR, storage-like flexibility and ramp-limited generation is not simply a collection of independent hourly feasible intervals.

The paper therefore focuses on two linked problems:

  • representation problem: derive a correct low-dimensional feasible region that preserves temporal coupling;
  • computational problem: remove redundant constraints and avoid exhaustive directional enumeration.

3. Overall framework — from internal DER constraints to a wholesale-market interface

The logic can be summarized as:

Internal local-market model
(network + DER + temporal constraints)
                ↓
Remove redundant internal constraints
using P-UCI
                ↓
Project the remaining high-dimensional model
onto PCC exchange variables
                ↓
Temporal-Coupled Feasible Region (TCFR)
                ↓
Wholesale market / ISO treats the local market
as one aggregated feasible resource

The information boundary is important. The wholesale market sees a feasible envelope for exchange power rather than the detailed schedules of every DER and every internal network variable.

The authors argue that this can reduce both computational burden and unnecessary disclosure of internal DER information. However, the paper does not formulate a cryptographic or Differential Privacy (DP) guarantee; its privacy benefit comes from sharing a condensed external representation instead of the full internal model.

4. Temporal-Coupled Feasible Region (TCFR) — what exactly is being projected?

The local electricity-market constraints are grouped into:

  • \(\Phi_L\): linearized power-flow, voltage, phase-angle and other network constraints;
  • \(\Phi_D\): DER capacity and other non-temporal operating limits;
  • \(\Phi_T\): temporal-coupled constraints, including DR and MT ramping constraints.

The complete model is written compactly as

\[ \Phi_A=\{(x,y)\mid Ax+By\le b\}, \]

where:

  • \(x\) contains the variables used to represent the local market to the outside, i.e. the relevant PCC exchange variables;
  • \(y\) contains internal variables such as load, line-flow and DER operating variables.

For a specified external exchange \(x\), the admissible internal schedules are

\[ Y(x)=\{y\mid By\le b-Ax\}. \]

The TCFR is then the projection of the complete feasible set onto \(x\):

\[ R_{\mathrm{TC}} =\mathrm{Pr}_x(\Phi_A) =\{x\mid \exists y: Ax+By\le b\} =\{x\mid Dx\le d\}. \]

This equation contains the central idea of the paper:

An exchange point \(x\) belongs to the TCFR only when at least one internal DER/network schedule \(y\) can realize it.

Therefore, aggregation here does not mean simply adding installed MW or independent flexibility intervals. It means preserving the existence of a feasible internal realization.

5. Feasibility diagnosis — finding exchange points that the local market cannot realize

To test whether a candidate exchange \(x\) is feasible, the authors introduce nonnegative slack vectors and solve

\[ f(x)= \min_{y,v^{I},v^{O}\ge0} \mathbf{1}^{\top}v^{I}+\mathbf{1}^{\top}v^{O} \]

subject to a relaxed form of the original internal constraints.

Interpretation:

  • \(f(x)=0\): no forced relaxation is needed, so an internal feasible schedule exists;
  • \(f(x)>0\): some constraints must be violated/relaxed, so the exchange point is outside the true TCFR.

The next question is more useful for region construction:

What is the worst infeasible point inside the current candidate region?

The authors formulate this as a max–min problem. They then use duality, strong duality and complementarity conditions, followed by a Big-\(M\) linearization, to obtain a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) diagnostic problem that can be handled by an off-the-shelf solver.

The important conceptual point is not the full algebra. The diagnostic model acts as a feasibility detector: it searches the current outer approximation for the exchange point that is hardest for the internal DER system to realize.

6. Outer progressive approximation — start large and cut away impossible exchange space

The paper constructs the TCFR through an outer progressive approximation.

The procedure is:

  1. Start from a reasonably large candidate region \(R_C\).
  2. Solve the diagnostic MILP to find the worst infeasible exchange point \(x^O\).
  3. If its infeasibility measure is zero, the current region contains no detected infeasible point and the algorithm stops.
  4. If \(x^O\) is infeasible, connect it to a known internal feasible point \(x^I\).
  5. Use dichotomy/bisection to locate a boundary point \(x^b\).
  6. Generate a new separating constraint (cut).
  7. Remove the infeasible part of \(R_C\) and repeat.

Geometrically:

large outer polytope
      ↓
find an impossible point
      ↓
locate the true boundary
      ↓
add one cut
      ↓
smaller polytope
      ↓
repeat until no infeasible point remains

This differs from simple directional enumeration. Instead of densely searching many directions in advance, the method uses detected infeasibility to decide where another boundary is needed.

7. Parallel Umbrella Constraint Identification (P-UCI) — remove constraints that never matter

Before repeated projection calculations, the authors reduce the original constraint set.

An umbrella constraint is an effective constraint whose hyperplane can touch the feasible region while all other constraints remain satisfied. A redundant constraint lies away from the feasible boundary and therefore does not affect the final feasible set.

For constraint \(j\), the method introduces a slack \(s_j\):

\[ s_j= \begin{cases} 0, & \text{constraint }j\text{ is umbrella},\\ >0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The geometric interpretation is intuitive:

  • \(s_j=0\): the constraint can become active on the feasible boundary;
  • \(s_j>0\): there is a positive distance between that constraint and the feasible region, so it is redundant for defining the boundary.

A direct UCI formulation becomes very large. If the original problem has \(I\) variables and \(J\) constraints, the paper states that the combined UCI model contains \(J(I+1)\) variables and \(J(J+1)\) constraints.

The proposed Parallel UCI (P-UCI) decomposes this into \(J\) independent Linear Programming (LP) subproblems. Each subproblem checks one constraint and contains only \(I+1\) variables and \(J+1\) constraints. Because these tests are independent, they can be solved in parallel.

Why this matters:

Projection is expensive partly because the algorithm repeatedly carries constraints that never define the feasible boundary. P-UCI removes those constraints before the more expensive region-characterization stage.

8. Modified Initial Space Generation (M-ISG) — a numerical detail that matters

Theoretically, a sufficiently large initial outer region should contain the true TCFR. In practice, the authors report that an excessively loose initial region may lead to missed boundaries because of solver accuracy.

They therefore propose Modified Initial Space Generation (M-ISG), which solves directional optimization problems to construct an initial region closer to the true feasible set.

A two-dimensional search direction is represented by

\[ \max \; x_1\cos\left(\frac{2i\pi}{N}\right) +x_2\sin\left(\frac{2i\pi}{N}\right), \]

subject to the local-market feasibility model.

The paper reports:

  • a very large generic initial region can miss two TCFR boundaries;
  • \(N=4\) M-ISG directions still miss some constraints;
  • \(N=8\) retrieves almost all boundaries in the illustrated example.

This is an important practical message: a mathematically correct projection framework can still be sensitive to numerical initialization and solver tolerance.

9. Case study setup

Modified IEEE 33-bus feeder

  • Test system: modified IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder.
  • Horizon: 24 hours.
  • Time step: 1 hour.
  • Local resources explicitly used in the base case: PV, MT and DR.
  • MTs: 5 units, each with 1 MW installed capacity.
  • MT ramp rate: 0.2 MW/h.
  • PVs: 7 units, each with 0.2 MW installed capacity.
  • Software: MATLAB R2016a Parallel Computing Toolbox.
  • Solver: IBM ILOG CPLEX 12.6.
  • Computer: Xeon Platinum 8160 CPU; the paper reports 3.50 GHz and 128 GB RAM.

The paper also tests a realistic radial distribution network in the metropolitan area of Caracas.

Caracas distribution network

  • Nodes: 141.
  • Maximum active load: 11.90 MW.
  • Maximum reactive load: 7.38 Mvar.
  • PVs: 80.
  • MTs: 20.

The paper does not report a field deployment or Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) experiment. The validation is computational.

10. Main findings

10.1 The local market’s feasible exchange region changes strongly over the day

The paper visualizes active/reactive feasible-region slices at 3:00, 8:00, 13:00, 18:00 and 23:00.

  • 3:00: the region is small because load is low, DR adjustment capability is limited and PV output is zero.
  • 8:00: increasing load and solar irradiance expand the feasible area.
  • 13:00: the feasible region is largest; high load and solar production increase the operating range, while reverse power flow and line limits affect its shape.
  • 18:00: lower PV output narrows active-power flexibility relative to 13:00.
  • 23:00: lower nighttime load reduces the region again.

The result shows why a fixed static aggregate capacity is insufficient: the local market’s external flexibility depends on both resource availability and network conditions.

10.2 Temporal coupling changes the geometry of aggregate flexibility

Because a 24-dimensional coupled region cannot be plotted directly, the paper shows a three-dimensional slice using active power at 11:00, 12:00 and 13:00.

If the three periods were independent, their combined feasible set would be a box/cube. Instead, the TCFR is an irregular polyhedron.

The cause is intertemporal physics and operational logic, particularly:

  • MT ramping constraints;
  • DR total-power/energy conservation across time.

This is one of the most important results in the paper:

Independent hourly flexibility regions can overstate what an aggregator can actually deliver across time.

10.3 The proposed representation dramatically reduces the information exchanged upward

For the 24-hour modified 33-bus case:

Representation stage Number of constraints
Original local-market scheduling problem 12,882
After P-UCI 8,430
Final projected TCFR 192

The final TCFR is therefore much more compact than the original local model.

The paper states that P-UCI reduces the “calculation pressure” by about 40%. A simple comparison of the reported constraint counts, however, gives a reduction from 12,882 to 8,430 of about 34.6%. The paper does not clarify whether “calculation pressure” refers to a broader computational measure rather than raw constraint count. This should therefore be treated as a wording/numerical point to check rather than silently reconciled.

10.4 P-UCI accelerates the feasible-region calculation without changing the region

Three methods are compared:

  • M1: directional enumeration;
  • M2: proposed feasible-region characterization without P-UCI;
  • M3: proposed characterization with P-UCI.

The reported pattern is:

  • with few enumeration directions, M1 is fast but inaccurate;
  • increasing the number of directions improves M1 accuracy but greatly increases computation time;
  • M3 is faster than M2;
  • M2 and M3 retain the same characterization accuracy because removing non-umbrella constraints does not change the true feasible boundary;
  • as the number/capacity of DERs increases, the number of effective TCFR boundaries grows and all methods require more computation.

The text available in the paper establishes these trends, but this note does not reproduce every numeric entry in Table I.

10.5 DER capacity does not expand flexibility in a purely proportional way

In the sensitivity analysis, increasing DER installed capacity generally enlarges the TCFR.

However:

  • between approximately 0.64 MW and 2.56 MW, the shape changes little;
  • when installed capacity exceeds 2.56 MW, the shape begins to change;
  • the paper identifies a boundary that visibly restricts further expansion and estimates that it is associated with a line-security constraint.

This demonstrates an important network effect:

More DER capacity does not automatically translate into proportional market flexibility. Once network constraints become active, the distribution grid limits how much of the additional resource can be exposed to the upper market.

The authors also note that it is difficult to assign a single physical interpretation to an individual TCFR facet because projection can combine multiple original physical constraints into one aggregate boundary.

10.6 The method remains advantageous on the larger Caracas network

For the 141-node Caracas case with 80 PVs and 20 MTs, computation becomes slower because of the larger system.

The paper reports that, relative to M1 with 64 directional segments, the proposed method improves computational efficiency by 246.4%.

The paper does not define this percentage in a way that allows it to be safely converted into a unique “time reduction” or “speed-up factor”, so the reported 246.4% value should be preserved as stated.

11. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — Aggregation is a feasibility-preservation problem, not a capacity-addition problem

A group of DERs cannot be represented correctly by simply summing maximum powers. The aggregate offer must guarantee that every accepted external exchange has at least one feasible internal realization.

Lesson 2 — Temporal coupling must survive aggregation

MT ramping and DR energy-conservation constraints connect different hours. Once these constraints are projected to the market interface, they create cross-time boundaries. Treating each hour independently can create infeasible wholesale schedules.

Lesson 3 — The distribution network is part of market flexibility

The sensitivity analysis shows that additional DER capacity eventually activates network-security limits. Therefore:

installed DER capacity
        ≠
deliverable market flexibility

The network determines how much flexibility can actually reach the PCC.

Lesson 4 — Redundant-constraint screening can be valuable before projection

P-UCI is a preprocessing step, but it directly improves the efficiency of the more expensive feasible-region extraction. Removing constraints that never become active does not change the feasible set, yet reduces repeated computational work.

Lesson 5 — Compact representation trades detail for a cleaner interface

TCFR gives the wholesale market only the information needed for feasible coordination. This reduces model size and unnecessary internal disclosure.

The trade-off is interpretability: a projected TCFR facet may combine several original constraints, making it difficult to say exactly which physical device or line “caused” that boundary.

Lesson 6 — Numerical geometry matters

The paper’s M-ISG discussion is easy to overlook but important. A poor initial outer region can cause missed boundaries in finite-precision computation even when the theoretical framework is sound.

12. Limitations / What remains unsolved

A. Limitations or unresolved issues explicitly visible in the paper

1. Physical interpretation of projected boundaries is difficult.
The paper explicitly states that a particular TCFR boundary is difficult to map back to one physical constraint because projection combines multiple original constraints.

2. Initial-space selection affects numerical boundary retrieval.
The paper reports that a very large initial space can miss boundaries and that even \(N=4\) M-ISG is insufficient in the illustrated example. \(N=8\) retrieves “almost all” boundaries, rather than an explicitly proven complete set under finite solver tolerance.

3. Larger systems still require more computation.
The Caracas case confirms that computation time increases with system scale, even though the proposed method is faster than the comparison method.

4. The paper does not give a detailed future-work agenda.
Its conclusion mainly summarizes the proposed representation and its potential use by distribution utilities and Independent System Operators (ISOs).

B. Further thought / possible extensions based on the model

The points below are not claims made by the authors; they are natural extensions from the paper’s formulation.

1. Deterministic TCFR → uncertainty-aware TCFR.
PV output and load are treated through a deterministic feasible-set formulation. A natural extension is a Stochastic Optimization, Robust Optimization, Chance-Constrained Optimization or Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) representation that gives a confidence/risk meaning to the aggregate feasible region.

2. Linearized network model → AC / unbalanced distribution-network representation.
The paper uses linearized power-flow constraints. For low-voltage or highly unbalanced systems, an AC or three-phase unbalanced feasible-region approximation with a quantified approximation error would be valuable.

3. Offline 24-hour representation → rolling/real-time update.
The paper defines the local electricity market as a real-time market, while the main case constructs a 24-hour TCFR. A practical extension is a rolling-horizon TCFR that updates quickly as forecasts, DER availability and network topology change.

4. Structural information hiding → formal privacy protection.
Sharing TCFR instead of the full internal model reduces disclosed information, but it is not a formal privacy guarantee. A future design could combine feasible-region exchange with differential privacy, secure multiparty computation or encrypted coordination while controlling the resulting feasibility error.

5. Compact boundary → interpretable boundary attribution.
Because a projected facet mixes multiple physical constraints, dual-information or attribution methods could identify which lines, devices or intertemporal constraints dominate each aggregate boundary.

6. Feasible-region representation → bidding, pricing and strategic behavior.
The current paper mainly solves the physical representation problem. A next step is to ask how a local market should bid a TCFR, how prices should be formed on its boundaries, and how market power or strategic misreporting of the feasible region should be controlled.

7. Upper-level dispatch → guaranteed fast disaggregation.
Once the ISO selects a point/trajectory inside the TCFR, the local operator still needs an internal DER schedule. The paper establishes existential feasibility, but a practically useful market architecture could jointly design compact aggregation and fast schedule recovery/disaggregation.

13. Research idea triggers

Idea 1 — Distributionally robust TCFR for local–wholesale market coordination

Deterministic TCFR
        +
PV/load forecast uncertainty
        +
Wasserstein DRO or joint chance constraints
        ↓
risk-guaranteed aggregate feasible region

Research question: How should the TCFR shrink or reshape when the local operator requires a specified out-of-sample feasibility probability?

This directly extends the paper without changing its core representation philosophy.

Idea 2 — TCFR + Distribution Locational Marginal Price (DLMP)

P026 provides a physical feasible interface, but it does not develop detailed local price formation.

A natural combined framework is:

network- and time-coupled TCFR
        ↓
wholesale/local coordinated clearing
        ↓
DLMP / uncertainty price / flexibility price

Research question: Can the shadow prices of TCFR boundaries be decomposed into network, temporal-flexibility and uncertainty components?

Idea 3 — Dynamic TCFR with incremental boundary updates

Instead of reconstructing the entire feasible region whenever forecasts change:

previous TCFR
      +
new PV/load forecast
      +
changed DER availability
      ↓
identify only affected umbrella constraints/facets
      ↓
fast updated TCFR

This is attractive for rolling-horizon and near-real-time market operation.

Idea 4 — Interpretable aggregate flexibility boundaries

Develop a method that maps each TCFR facet back to its dominant physical causes:

  • line congestion;
  • voltage constraint;
  • MT ramp;
  • DR energy budget;
  • DER capacity.

This would make the aggregate market representation more useful for operators, because a boundary would not only say “cannot go further” but also explain why.

Idea 5 — Strategic TCFR reporting and market power

The method assumes that the local market submits its feasible region as a truthful technical representation.

A market-design extension could study:

  • intentional shrinking of the declared feasible region;
  • strategic withholding of flexibility;
  • manipulation of aggregate boundaries;
  • auditing or incentive mechanisms that make truthful feasible-region reporting desirable.

Idea 6 — Aggregation + exact/fast disaggregation as one design problem

A strong extension would require that every wholesale schedule accepted inside the aggregate region can be converted into individual DER setpoints within a strict time limit.

This connects market abstraction to real implementation:

wholesale dispatch
      ↓
TCFR point
      ↓
fast internal disaggregation
      ↓
DER/network-feasible schedule

14. Critical reading notes

  • Constraint-count wording: the paper reports 12,882 original constraints and 8,430 after P-UCI, while describing the reduction in “calculation pressure” as about 40%. The raw count reduction is approximately 34.6%. The paper does not explain whether “calculation pressure” is intended to mean something broader than constraint count.
  • Equation-reference issue: in the prose explaining Fig. 3 and UCI, the paper states that \(s_j>0\) is forced “to satisfy Eq. (11)”. Eq. (11) belongs to the earlier strong-duality derivation, whereas the surrounding UCI discussion concerns Eqs. (15)–(17). This appears to be a possible equation-number reference inconsistency; it should not be silently corrected.
  • Initialization sensitivity: the paper says \(N=8\) retrieves “almost all” boundaries in the illustrated M-ISG test. This is weaker than a finite-precision guarantee that every boundary is recovered.
  • 246.4% efficiency statement: the paper reports a 246.4% computational-efficiency improvement on the Caracas network but does not provide a sufficiently explicit definition in the surrounding text to translate this safely into a unique speed-up or percentage time saving.
  • Privacy wording: the conclusion states that DER users can avoid disclosure of private information by using the aggregate TCFR. This should be understood as reduced model-information disclosure; the paper does not provide a formal privacy metric or privacy-preserving protocol.

Problem-map tags: local–wholesale market coordination · flexibility aggregation · temporal coupling · feasible-region projection · network constraints · constraint redundancy · scalability · information disclosure · physical interpretability · real-time updating

注记[P027] Yu et al. (2023) — Frequency Regulation Capacity Offering of District Cooling System: An Intrinsic-Motivated Reinforcement Learning Method

Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, 14(4), 2762–2773
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3220732
Main topics: district cooling system (DCS) · frequency regulation · regulation-capacity offering · Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) · Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) · intrinsic motivation · pseudo-count exploration · thermal inertia · demand response · PJM regulation market

Quick takeaway

This paper studies a question that is easy to state but difficult to solve in practice: how much frequency-regulation capacity should a District Cooling System (DCS) offer one hour ahead? Offering too little wastes the large thermal flexibility of the cooling system and reduces market revenue. Offering too much can make the DCS unable to follow the regulation signal, lower its performance score, and potentially violate building comfort requirements.

The problem is difficult because a DCS is not a simple controllable load. Its cooling station, pipelines, heat exchangers and buildings create thermal inertia, ramp limits and transportation delay. In addition, building cooling demand and real-time regulation signals are stochastic. The authors therefore formulate the hour-ahead capacity-offering problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and use a model-free Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) agent to choose the continuous regulation-capacity offer.

The distinctive contribution is not only using DRL, but adding intrinsic motivation based on a pseudo-count of visited states. Rarely visited states receive an exploration bonus, encouraging the agent to explore the state space more efficiently. In the reported simulations, this reduces score-constraint violations during training and produces a better converged policy than standard DDPG.

The paper is especially useful for understanding three ideas: (1) flexible thermal loads can be market resources, not only energy consumers; (2) regulation-capacity offering is a sequential decision problem because thermal flexibility is time-coupled; and (3) “model-free” DRL does not mean that physical feasibility disappears — the agent still interacts with a physical/simulation environment that determines temperature, power and regulation performance.

1. Problem addressed — how much regulation capacity can a DCS safely offer?

A DCS supplies chilled water from one central energy station to multiple buildings. Because buildings and water networks have substantial thermal inertia, the electrical consumption of chillers can be temporarily moved up or down without immediately violating indoor-temperature requirements.

This makes a DCS potentially valuable for frequency regulation. However, the market requires the resource to declare its regulation capacity in advance and then follow the system operator’s real-time signal. The key decision is therefore not simply whether the DCS is flexible, but:

Given the current thermal state, recent market information and uncertain future signals, what regulation capacity should the DCS offer for the next operating hour?

The decision contains a basic economic trade-off:

larger offered capacity
        ↓
higher possible regulation revenue
        ↓
more difficult signal tracking
        ↓
higher risk of low performance score / comfort problems

The paper therefore aims to maximize cumulative regulation revenue while maintaining market-service quality and building comfort.

2. Why existing approaches are not enough

The authors identify three main difficulties.

2.1 Complex physical dynamics

A DCS is a networked thermal system. Cooling is generated at the energy station and transported through long pipelines to multiple buildings. Important dynamics include:

  • chiller electricity-to-cooling conversion;
  • water mass-flow control;
  • building thermal capacity and resistance;
  • pipeline transportation delay;
  • water-flow inertia and ramp limits;
  • uncertain internal building heat gains.

The authors argue that accurate parameters are difficult to obtain and change with environmental conditions. Therefore, detailed model-based optimization may be difficult to apply directly to a real DCS.

2.2 Regulation capacity is time-coupled

Thermal inertia behaves somewhat like limited energy storage. If the DCS continuously provides one-direction regulation, the buildings may gradually approach their comfort limits. Therefore, using flexibility now changes the amount of flexibility available later.

This means that a myopic strategy that only maximizes the next hour’s revenue can be poor. The controller needs to consider current and future rewards.

2.3 Cooling demand and regulation signals are uncertain

Two major uncertainties are emphasized:

  • random human behavior changes building cooling demand;
  • real-time regulation signals are stochastic and difficult to predict precisely.

The probability distributions are not assumed to be known in a form convenient for stochastic optimization. This motivates a data-driven sequential decision method.

3. Physical mechanism — why a cooling system can provide frequency regulation

The DCS considered in the paper consists of one energy station, pipelines, heat exchangers and multiple buildings.

The chillers convert electrical power into cooling. In simplified form,

\[ P^{\mathrm{ch}}_t = \frac{Q^{\mathrm{ch}}_t}{\mathrm{COP}}, \]

where \(P^{\mathrm{ch}}_t\) is chiller electrical power, \(Q^{\mathrm{ch}}_t\) is cooling power and COP is the coefficient of performance.

Building indoor temperature follows a thermal-balance equation of the form

\[ D_i\frac{\partial T^A_{i,t}}{\partial t} = \frac{T^O_t-T^A_{i,t}}{R_i} +\zeta_{i,t} -\eta^{II}_i Q_{i,t}. \]

Here:

  • \(D_i\): thermal capacity of building \(i\);
  • \(R_i\): thermal resistance;
  • \(T^A_{i,t}\): indoor air temperature;
  • \(T^O_t\): ambient temperature;
  • \(\zeta_{i,t}\): uncertain internal heat load;
  • \(Q_{i,t}\): cooling delivered to the building.

The practical meaning is more important than the exact equation: indoor temperature does not respond instantaneously to chiller power. This delay creates a short-term buffer that can be used for grid regulation.

The paper also models water-flow ramp limits, inertia and pipeline transportation delay. Therefore, regulation capacity is constrained not only by instantaneous chiller power but also by the recent operating history of the DCS.

4. Market layer — the DCS sells regulation capacity to PJM

The paper uses the PJM regulation-market mechanism as the market setting. The DCS can revise its regulation-capacity offer until 60 minutes before the operating hour.

The hourly regulation revenue is modeled as

\[ r^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t = C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t p^{\mathrm{PJM}}_t, \]

where:

  • \(C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t\): offered regulation capacity;
  • \(s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t\in[0,1]\): performance score;
  • \(p^{\mathrm{PJM}}_t\): regulation market-clearing price.

The DCS is assumed to be a price-taker.

The performance score combines three aspects used by PJM:

  1. precision;
  2. correlation;
  3. response delay.

The paper adopts 0.75 as the required score because it is the PJM qualification-test threshold and is stricter than the 0.4 daily disqualification threshold discussed by the authors.

The optimization goal is conceptually

\[ \max \sum_t C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t p^{\mathrm{PJM}}_t \]

subject to

\[ s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t\ge 0.75, \qquad |T^A_{i,t}-T^{\mathrm{set}}_{i,t}|\le \Delta T_i. \]

Thus, the largest possible capacity offer is not automatically the best offer. A large offer can reduce the performance score and eventually reduce total revenue.

5. MDP formulation — converting capacity offering into a sequential decision problem

The paper formulates the problem as a 5-tuple MDP \(\langle S,A,P,R,\gamma\rangle\).

5.1 Action — one continuous hour-ahead capacity offer

The action is

\[ a_t=C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t. \]

It is a continuous variable. During the following operating hour, the real-time regulation signal lies in \([-1,1]\), so the DCS should be able to modulate power approximately within \([-a_t,a_t]\) around its baseline.

This continuous action space is one reason the paper selects DDPG rather than a discrete-action method such as a basic DQN.

5.2 State — only information considered highly relevant to the offer

The state contains six elements:

\[ s_t= \left[ t, p^{\mathrm{PJM}}_{t-1}, P^{\mathrm{ch}}_{t-1}, \mathbb{E}[\Delta T_{i,t-1}], \mathbb{E}[\sigma^s_{t-1}], f(\sigma^s_{t-1}) \right]^T. \]

Their roles are:

State variable Why it matters
time \(t\) indirectly represents daily patterns of ambient temperature and cooling demand
previous market price provides recent market information
previous DCS power indicates available up/down regulation headroom
mean indoor-temperature deviation measures comfort state and remaining thermal flexibility
mean previous regulation signal summarizes signal direction/intensity
maximum cumulative regulation feature represents how strongly the previous signal continuously pushed the DCS in one direction

The authors deliberately do not include every DCS physical state. They treat omitted information as environmental uncertainty in order to simplify learning.

5.3 Reward — revenue when qualified, penalty when the score is violated

The DRL reward is

\[ R_t = \beta_1\kappa_t C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t p_t - \beta_2(1-\kappa_t)\frac{C^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t}{s^{\mathrm{DCS}}_t}, \]

where \(\kappa_t=1\) when the performance score satisfies the requirement and \(0\) otherwise.

The first term rewards profitable qualified participation. The second term penalizes an offer that causes the performance score to fall below the required level.

The discount factor \(\gamma\) makes the agent value future rewards, which is important because thermal flexibility used now changes future regulation capability.

6. Why DDPG is used

Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) is an actor–critic DRL algorithm for continuous actions.

The actor learns the mapping

observed DCS/market state → regulation-capacity offer

while the critic estimates the long-term value of a state–action pair.

The agent learns from transitions

\[ (s_t,a_t,R_t,s_{t+1}) \]

stored in an experience replay buffer. The policy is updated to make high-value actions more likely.

The important interpretation is that DDPG allows the controller to learn the combined consequences of:

  • offering a large or small regulation capacity;
  • the future thermal state;
  • uncertain market signals;
  • uncertain building cooling demand;
  • the resulting market performance score.

The DRL agent itself does not use the explicit DCS equations when deciding the action. However, in the paper’s numerical study, those physical equations are used to construct the simulation environment with which the agent interacts.

7. Core contribution — pseudo-count intrinsic motivation

A standard model-free DRL agent initially knows little about the environment. It therefore requires many trial-and-error interactions. In a physical energy system, poor exploration can produce unacceptable operating decisions.

The authors add intrinsic motivation to encourage more efficient exploration.

The intuitive idea is:

frequently visited state
    → little new information
    → small exploration bonus

rarely visited state
    → more new information
    → large exploration bonus

For discrete states, this could be implemented by counting visits directly. The DCS state is continuous, so exact states are almost never repeated. The paper therefore estimates a pseudo-count using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) density estimator.

The pseudo-count is calculated from the state probability before and after re-observing the state:

\[ \hat N_n(s_t) = \frac{\rho_n(s_t)[1-\rho'_n(s_t)]} {\rho'_n(s_t)-\rho_n(s_t)}. \]

The empirical reward is then augmented by

\[ R_t^+ = R_t + \beta_3\left(\hat N_n(s_t)+0.01\right)^{-1/2}. \]

A small pseudo-count produces a large bonus. Therefore, the agent is encouraged to visit less familiar regions of the state space instead of repeatedly exploring already familiar situations.

The goal is not to make exploration more aggressive. The goal is to cover useful state space in fewer episodes so that the agent requires fewer harmful trial-and-error interactions overall.

8. Overall strategy — market operation and DRL training are linked

The operating loop is:

observe DCS + market state
        ↓
agent offers one-hour regulation capacity
        ↓
DCS follows real-time regulation signal
        ↓
market calculates performance and revenue
        ↓
DCS state changes
        ↓
transition is stored for learning

During training, intrinsic motivation modifies the reward used for policy updates. During actual operation, the economic revenue and physical response still come from the DCS/market environment.

9. Case study setup

9.1 Physical system

  • DCS basis: realistic system schematic from Hengqin, China.
  • Simulation environment: one energy station and 12 connected buildings.
  • Total cooling capacity: 144 MW.
  • COP: 5.
  • Heat-transfer efficiencies: 90%.
  • Building thermal capacity: approximately \(10^6\)–\(10^7\) kJ/°C.
  • Building thermal resistance: approximately 0.001–0.003 °C/kW.
  • Indoor set temperature: 20–23 °C.
  • Comfort range: ±1 °C.
  • DCS parameters are based on system technical guidelines and several Chinese national/local standards.

9.2 Market data

  • Market: PJM frequency regulation.
  • Regulation signal: real PJM RegA data.
  • Hourly regulation price: real PJM data.
  • Required performance score: 0.75.
  • Minimum market-access capacity: 1 MW.

The physical DCS is Chinese while the market data/rules are from PJM. The study therefore combines a realistic DCS-based simulation environment with real market data rather than reproducing one existing field deployment.

9.3 Compared methods

  • B1: proposed DDPG + pseudo-count intrinsic motivation.
  • B2: standard DDPG without intrinsic motivation.
  • B3: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)-based heuristic strategy.
  • B4: equal-proportional offering based on recent DCS power, tested at 10%, 20% and 30%.

9.4 DRL training settings

  • training episodes: 7500;
  • discount factor: \(\gamma=0.9\);
  • mini-batch size: 200;
  • actor hidden layers: 128 × 128;
  • critic hidden layers: 128 × 128;
  • actor learning rate: 0.001;
  • critic learning rate: 0.0001;
  • target-network smooth factor: 0.005;
  • exploration noise: Gaussian with \(\sigma=0.3\);
  • reward weights: \(\beta_1=0.005\), \(\beta_2=0.003\), \(\beta_3=0.05\);
  • implementation: Python/PyTorch, Intel Core i7 3.0 GHz, 16 GB memory.

The paper states that \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\) and \(\beta_3\) were selected sequentially through reward-scale adjustment, penalty tuning and a coarse parameter sweep.

10. Main findings

10.1 Intrinsic motivation improves training efficiency and reduces unsafe exploration

Both B1 and B2 start from the same random policy and interact with the same simulation environment.

The authors report that:

  • both agents become relatively stable after roughly 2000 episodes;
  • B1 obtains higher episode rewards during training;
  • the final converged reward of B1 is higher than B2;
  • B2 continues to violate the performance-score requirement frequently during training;
  • B1 avoids significant score violations after approximately 150 episodes.

The authors explicitly state that neither converged DRL policy is guaranteed to be the global optimum.

The key point is therefore not “B1 finds the mathematical optimum,” but:

Intrinsic motivation reaches a useful policy with fewer harmful trial-and-error interactions.

10.2 A fixed percentage of DCS power is not an effective capacity-offering rule

The equal-proportional strategies expose a clear trade-off:

  • B4-10%: conservative, good performance score, but low revenue;
  • B4-30%: aggressive, many score violations and reduced revenue;
  • B4-20%: better balance, but still inferior to the learned policies.

This shows that the best regulation offer is state-dependent, not a fixed percentage of current or historical power.

10.3 DRL outperforms the heuristic and proportional benchmarks

The paper evaluates the trained policies over two months of simulated operation.

The reported ranking is clear:

  • B1 has the highest average daily revenue;
  • B1 also has the smallest daily score-violation hours;
  • B2 is second best;
  • PSO performs better than the fixed-percentage strategies but worse than the two RL methods.

The reason given by the authors is that the learned agents use the DCS operating state and historical signal information to decide whether and how strongly to participate. They can therefore exploit thermal inertia through intermittent participation instead of blindly providing regulation every hour.

10.4 The DCS should not regulate continuously for too long

On a representative operating day under B1:

  • the DCS participates in the regulation market for 15 hours;
  • the longest continuous regulation period is 4 hours;
  • after several hours of regulation, the policy tends to stop temporarily and allow thermal flexibility to recover.

This behavior is physically meaningful. Thermal inertia is a limited flexibility resource, similar in some respects to an energy buffer. Continuous regulation can gradually push indoor temperatures toward their limits.

10.5 About 20% of operating power is a useful empirical scale, but not a fixed optimal rule

From the numerical experiments, the authors state that the DCS can provide approximately 20% of its operating power as regulation capacity.

This should not be interpreted as a universal constant. The rest of the paper shows that the optimal offer changes with thermal state, time of day and regulation-signal characteristics.

10.6 Night-time capacity is more stable than daytime capacity

The authors observe that regulation-capacity offering during 22:00–08:00 is more stable than during the daytime.

The explanation is that daytime human occupancy creates more uncertain and diverse internal cooling loads, which makes building temperatures and available flexibility more variable.

10.7 Comfort is maintained in the tested operation

For the representative summer day:

  • ambient temperature varies approximately 28–32 °C;
  • building set temperatures are 20–23 °C;
  • required comfort range is ±1 °C;
  • all reported building temperature deviations remain within the required range under B1.

This result is important because high regulation revenue would not be useful if it were obtained by sacrificing the cooling service that the DCS exists to provide.

11. Additional regulation cost — the paper’s supplementary check

The main objective does not include additional electricity cost or equipment degradation from regulation. The authors justify this assumption with an additional analysis.

Using one week of simulated operating data:

  • maximum daily power-consumption deviation between regulation and non-regulation operation is about 4.30%;
  • average difference is −13.2 MWh, approximately −0.70% of average daily electricity consumption.

The authors therefore argue that additional energy consumption is small because regulation makes power fluctuate around the original baseline rather than continuously increasing consumption.

For equipment degradation, the paper does not build a quantitative lifetime model. It argues that compressor adjustment intervals remain the same and that ramp/time-delay limits prevent excessive adjustment. Hardware degradation is therefore assumed to be negligible in the main formulation.

12. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — Flexibility value depends on what you promise, not only what you physically possess

A DCS may have large thermal flexibility, but the market problem is to choose a capacity that can be reliably delivered. Over-offering can be economically worse than conservative participation because poor tracking lowers the performance score.

Lesson 2 — Thermal flexibility is an intertemporal resource

The DCS cannot provide the same regulation capability indefinitely. Using thermal headroom now changes what remains later. Therefore, capacity offering naturally becomes a sequential optimization problem.

Lesson 3 — Market participation and physical operation must be studied together

A market offer affects real chiller operation, indoor temperatures and future flexibility. A purely economic bidding model that ignores these physical states can generate unrealistic offers.

Lesson 4 — “Model-free” means the policy does not require an explicit model, not that physics is irrelevant

The DDPG agent does not solve the DCS equations online. Nevertheless, its reward and next state still depend on physical system dynamics. In the paper, these dynamics are represented by a detailed simulation model.

Lesson 5 — Safer exploration is different from safe control

The proposed intrinsic motivation reduces the number of constraint violations during learning. The authors explicitly acknowledge that it cannot guarantee zero violation of hard constraints.

This distinction is important:

fewer unsafe trials
        ≠
formal safety guarantee

Lesson 6 — Intermittent market participation can be better than continuous participation

The learned strategy frequently pauses regulation after several hours. The pause restores thermal headroom and enables later profitable participation. Flexibility scheduling is therefore partly a problem of when not to participate.

13. Limitations / What remains unsolved

A. Limitations and future work explicitly stated by the authors

1. No strict safety guarantee.
The intrinsic-motivation method only decreases constraint violations by improving training efficiency. It is intended for soft-constraint problems and cannot guarantee zero hard-constraint violations.

2. Early online training is still unstable.
At the beginning of training, reward is low and score violations can be substantial. The authors suggest high-quality pretraining and transfer learning as an important future direction.

3. Simulation-to-reality gap remains.
