B. Further research space visible from the model

Price-taking assumption. The data center only responds to an exogenous price. The paper does not study strategic bidding, market clearing, demand-response payment, or the effect of a large data center on Locational Marginal Price (LMP).

No grid-network constraints. The power system appears only through a price signal. Distribution-network congestion, voltage limits, feeder capacity, and network-aware flexibility are not modeled.

Simulation rather than field deployment. The simulator is driven by real traces, but the paper does not report Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) or live data-center deployment.

No explicit storage or on-site generation. Flexible computing is the only major flexibility mechanism in the main model.

No formal safe-exploration constraint. SLA violations are handled through reward penalties rather than hard safety constraints or chance constraints.

Scheduler abstraction. The environment model learns aggregate scheduler behavior, but the generalization to entirely new schedulers, hardware configurations, or unseen workload classes is not theoretically guaranteed.

Optimality bound is not an online certificate. The theoretical gap depends on quantities such as environment-model error and concentrability. The paper establishes the bound analytically but does not demonstrate a practical real-time procedure that computes a certified bound during operation.

14. Research idea triggers

Idea 1 — From price-taking load response to market participation

Extend the framework from “receive price → adjust cap” to data-center bidding in day-ahead / real-time / ancillary-service markets. The research question becomes whether computing flexibility can be priced and offered as a market product while still respecting SLA uncertainty.

Idea 2 — Network-aware data-center flexibility

Add distribution-network constraints or Distribution Locational Marginal Prices (DLMPs). This would connect computing flexibility to feeder congestion and voltage management rather than treating the electricity system as an external scalar price.

Idea 3 — Risk-sensitive distributional MBRL

The paper already learns the return distribution. A natural extension is to use the distribution explicitly in decision-making, for example through CVaR, chance constraints, or tail-probability limits on SLA violations.

Idea 4 — Joint power capping + ESS optimization

This is the most direct extension mentioned by the authors. Flexible jobs provide temporal computing flexibility, while batteries provide electrical energy flexibility. A joint controller could decide whether to defer jobs, discharge storage, or accept a higher electricity price.

Idea 5 — Price + carbon + renewable matching

The paper notes that carbon intensity or renewable profiles could replace price signals. A stronger extension is a multi-objective controller using electricity price + marginal carbon intensity + renewable availability + SLA cost simultaneously.

Idea 6 — Continual learning with explicit change detection

The experiments contain scheduler changes, job bursts, and price spikes, but the method reacts implicitly. A new design could add drift/change-point detection and trigger selective model adaptation, model reset, or uncertainty inflation when the environment changes structurally.

Idea 7 — Formal privacy for aggregated feedback

Replace the informal “aggregated information” privacy argument with a measurable privacy mechanism. The energy manager could learn from differentially private or encrypted aggregate feedback and quantify the trade-off between privacy, model accuracy, and energy cost.

Idea 8 — Safe or offline RL for deployment

Because real exploration is expensive, a practical next step is offline pretraining from historical traces, followed by constrained online adaptation. Hard SLA constraints, safe exploration, or fallback rules could make deployment more credible.

Idea 9 — More realistic power-cap wear and ramping model

Replace the current capping-intensity penalty with explicit cap-ramp limits, switching/ramping costs, thermal effects, and hardware reliability models. This would align the mathematical penalty more directly with the hardware-wear motivation.

15. One-sentence memory hook

This paper learns how a hidden cloud scheduler reacts to an aggregate power cap, then uses an uncertainty-aware MBRL controller to shift computing demand toward favorable electricity-price periods with fewer real interactions.

Problem-map tags: data-center demand flexibility · incomplete operational information · power capping · SLA-energy trade-off · sample efficiency · dynamic scheduler · environment uncertainty · model-based reinforcement learning · decision-aware model learning · privacy boundary · price-responsive demand · safe deployment

注记[P031] Ye et al. (2023) — Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coordinated Energy Trading and Flexibility Services Provision in Local Electricity Markets

Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, Vol. 14, No. 2, March 2023, pp. 1541–1554
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3149266
Main topics: Local Electricity Market (LEM); local energy trading; Flexibility Services (FS); prosumer coordination; Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (MADRL); Multi-Actor-Attention-Critic (MAAC); Prioritized Experience Replay (PER); Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE); Electric Vehicles (EV); Energy Storage (ES); Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC)

Quick takeaway

This paper studies a Local Electricity Market (LEM) that performs two functions at the same time: prosumers trade energy locally, and their flexible Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) sell upward/downward flexibility services to an Electricity System Operator (ESO) or Distribution System Operator (DSO). The central question is not only how to operate flexible DERs economically, but how to coordinate many heterogeneous prosumers without requiring a central entity to know every household’s detailed DER model and private operating information.

The paper develops two formulations of the same problem. First, it builds an idealized model-based, system-centric optimization that jointly optimizes energy trading and flexibility provision and explicitly models the time-coupled constraints of EVs, batteries and HVAC systems. This serves as a theoretical benchmark. Second, it reformulates the problem as a model-free, prosumer-centric Markov Game, where each prosumer is an agent that learns its own policy from observations and interaction with the environment.

The proposed learning method, MAAC-PER, combines the Multi-Actor-Attention-Critic (MAAC) architecture with Prioritized Experience Replay (PER). MAAC is used to reduce multi-agent non-stationarity and scalability/privacy problems, while PER accelerates learning by replaying more informative experiences. In a 300-prosumer case study using Ausgrid data, the learned solution is only 2.70% / 3.35% above the theoretical benchmark for the LEM / LEM+FS cases, respectively, while avoiding the perfect-model and perfect-forecast assumptions of the benchmark.

1. Problem addressed — how can a LEM coordinate both energy trading and flexibility services?

The paper starts from a practical DER-management problem. Large numbers of small flexible resources are increasingly owned by individual prosumers. Coordinating them centrally is difficult because the system would need to collect detailed operating models, forecasts and private information from many households.

A Local Electricity Market reduces this system-wide coordination problem to a smaller local cluster. However, many existing LEM studies focus mainly on local energy trading: prosumers use local surplus PV and flexible resources to reduce imports from the grid and improve collective self-consumption.

The authors argue that this leaves another source of value underused. Flexible DERs can also provide flexibility services (FS) to the wider electricity system, such as balancing or distribution-network support. Therefore, the research problem is:

How can heterogeneous prosumers coordinate their DERs so that local energy trading and external flexibility-service provision are optimized jointly, while avoiding a centralized architecture that requires full models, forecasts and private data?

The two market functions compete for the same physical flexibility. A battery, EV or HVAC system used to improve local self-consumption has less remaining flexibility available for FS, and vice versa. This makes joint optimization important.

2. Why existing approaches are not enough

The literature review is organized around three dimensions.

2.1 System-centric vs. prosumer-centric coordination

A system-centric architecture can theoretically achieve a globally optimal solution because a central coordinator knows all DER models and dispatches them directly. The authors highlight four practical drawbacks: communication burden, computational burden, privacy concerns and reliability concerns.

A prosumer-centric architecture leaves DER dispatch authority with individual prosumers and uses market signals to coordinate them indirectly. It is more practical but generally cannot guarantee the system-wide optimum.

2.2 Model-based vs. model-free decision-making

Most model-based methods require:

  • explicit knowledge of complex DER operating models;
  • accurate forecasts of uncertain variables such as demand and PV output; or
  • known analytical uncertainty distributions.

The authors argue that these requirements create large monitoring, forecasting and computational burdens.

Model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) avoids explicit DER models in the agent decision process. However, multi-agent learning introduces its own problems. Concurrent independent learning suffers from a non-stationary environment. Fully centralized learning and Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) can become computationally intractable and may require private information from all agents. Parameter-sharing methods assume homogeneous agents, which does not fit heterogeneous DER portfolios.

2.3 Energy trading and flexibility services are often separated

Most prior LEM work focuses on energy trading only. A smaller body of work studies flexibility markets. Very few studies combine both functions, and the paper identifies specific limitations in those that do:

  • time-coupled DER constraints are sometimes ignored;
  • energy and FS are sometimes optimized sequentially rather than simultaneously;
  • some reserve-market designs are not aligned with ESO/DSO procurement structures.

The paper therefore identifies the missing combination as:

prosumer-centric + model-free + simultaneous local energy trading and FS provision.

3. Overall LEM architecture — two markets compete for the same DER flexibility

The LEM contains residential prosumers with heterogeneous portfolios that may include PV, inflexible demand, EVs, ES units and HVAC systems. A LEM platform connects these prosumers with an electricity supplier and an ESO/DSO.

The architecture contains three main flow types:

  • energy flows: local energy trading among prosumers and residual import/export with the supplier;
  • FS flows: aggregated upward/downward flexibility sold to the ESO/DSO;
  • information flows: retail tariffs, FS prices and local market information communicated through the LEM platform.

The coordination horizon is one day with a 30-minute resolution, so \(T=48\) periods.

The two generic FS products are:

  • up-FS: increase generation or reduce demand relative to the baseline;
  • down-FS: reduce generation or increase demand relative to the baseline.

The paper models only the forward availability of this flexibility. It does not model real-time activation or activation remuneration. The authors also state that the generic FS representation does not capture special services such as dynamic frequency response or reactive-power management.

4. Model-based system-centric benchmark

The benchmark assumes that a central coordinator has perfect knowledge of all DER operating models and accurate forecasts of uncertain exogenous variables.

4.1 EV and battery flexibility

EV and ES flexibility comes from changing charging/discharging schedules while respecting inter-temporal energy constraints. For an EV, the basic energy-balance relation is

\[ E^{ev}_{n,t}=E^{ev}_{n,t-1}+\Delta t P^{evc}_{n,t}\eta^{evc}_{n} -\Delta t P^{evd}_{n,t}/\eta^{evd}_{n}-E^{tr}_{n,t}. \]

This equation links present actions to future flexibility: charging or discharging now changes the energy margin available later. EVs additionally have availability and departure-energy requirements. ES units follow a similar model but are always grid-connected and have no commuting-energy requirement.

The up-/down-FS limits are constrained not only by charging/discharging power capacity but also by the battery’s remaining energy margin. Therefore, the paper explicitly captures the time-coupled physical nature of flexibility.

4.2 HVAC flexibility

HVAC flexibility is represented through indoor thermal dynamics. HVAC power can be shifted as long as indoor temperature remains within user comfort limits. This means thermal comfort acts as an energy-like storage constraint: consuming less/more power now changes the future temperature margin available for FS.

4.3 System-level objective

The LEM net power exchange with the external supplier is the sum of the prosumers’ net demands:

\[ P_t^{re}=\sum_{n=1}^{N} l_{n,t}. \]

The benchmark minimizes

\[ \min \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left[ \lambda_t^b[P_t^{re}]^+ +\lambda_t^s[P_t^{re}]^- -\lambda_t^{F,u}FU_t^{tot} -\lambda_t^{F,d}FD_t^{tot} \right]. \]

The first two terms represent the cost/revenue of residual grid import/export. The last two terms represent revenue from selling upward and downward flexibility. Importantly, local energy trading and FS provision are optimized simultaneously, so the optimizer decides how much DER flexibility should be used for each purpose.

5. Model-free prosumer-centric reformulation as a Markov Game

The practical formulation treats each prosumer as an agent in a finite Markov Game (MG). Unlike the benchmark, an agent does not explicitly know its DER equations when selecting actions. Physical constraints are imposed ex post by the environment after the agent proposes an action.

5.1 Observation — local information plus 48-step history

Each prosumer observes its own local variables, including EV/ES energy states, EV availability, indoor temperature, and historical profiles of:

  • outdoor temperature;
  • retail import/export tariffs;
  • up-/down-FS prices;
  • inflexible demand;
  • PV production.

For these time-series variables, the previous 48 half-hour periods are included. A Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network extracts features intended to infer future trends without using external forecasts.

The global state is conceptually the concatenation of all agents’ observations, but each agent can physically observe only its own local information.

5.2 Actions — energy operation and FS provision

For each flexible DER, actions are continuous normalized commands. EV/ES actions include charging/discharging plus upward/downward FS decisions. HVAC actions include power consumption plus upward/downward FS provision.

The environment maps normalized actions to physically feasible power levels using the relevant power, energy or thermal limits. This design is important: the policy itself is model-free, but the simulated environment still contains the physical models needed to enforce feasibility.

An exception is the EV departure-energy requirement. It is not hard-enforced by the immediate action projection; violation is instead penalized in the reward at departure.

6. Local energy pricing and agent economic objective

Local energy prices are set with a Mid-Market Rate (MMR) mechanism. The base local price is the midpoint of the supplier’s retail import and export tariffs, and the actual local buying/selling prices are adjusted according to whether the LEM as a whole is a net consumer or net producer.

This mechanism creates a price between the retail buying and selling alternatives, allowing both local buyers and sellers to potentially benefit from local trading.

For prosumer \(n\), the paper defines the net-cost expression as

\[ r^{net}_{n,t} =\lambda_t^{L,b}[l_{n,t}]^+ +\lambda_t^{L,s}[l_{n,t}]^- -\left(\lambda_t^{F,u}FU^{pro}_{n,t} +\lambda_t^{F,d}FD^{pro}_{n,t}\right). \]

An EV departure penalty is added when the required commuting energy is not available.

Critical reading note: the paper calls this quantity a reward and states that agents maximize cumulative reward, but the expression itself is written as a net cost (positive import cost minus revenues). As written, maximizing it would appear to favor a higher cost. The paper does not explicitly reconcile this sign convention. This may be a notation/sign issue in the manuscript or a difference between the written formulation and implementation, but it should not be silently corrected.

7. MAAC — using attention to coordinate many heterogeneous agents

The proposed method builds on the Multi-Actor-Attention-Critic (MAAC) architecture, which follows Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE).

During training, each agent has its own actor and critic. Rather than feeding every other agent’s full observation/action vector directly into agent \(n\)’s critic, MAAC learns a compressed, attention-weighted contribution from the other population:

\[ x_n=\sum_{j\ne n}\omega_j v_j. \]

The attention weight \(\omega_j\) determines how strongly agent \(n\)’s critic should consider information associated with agent \(j\). Therefore, the critic can focus on the other agents that are most relevant to its value estimate instead of treating every agent equally.

The paper argues that this helps with three problems:

  1. non-stationarity: other agents’ behavior is incorporated into centralized training;
  2. scalability: the critic avoids direct concatenation of all raw observations/actions;
  3. privacy: the platform handles learned embeddings/contributions rather than requiring agents to directly exchange their full local physical information.

8. MAAC-PER — prioritize informative experiences

The paper further combines MAAC with Prioritized Experience Replay (PER). Instead of sampling all historical experiences uniformly, experiences with larger Temporal-Difference (TD) errors are replayed more frequently.

The sampling probability is

\[ P_l=\frac{p_l^{\beta_1}}{\sum_j p_j^{\beta_1}}, \]

where the priority is rank-based on the absolute TD error. Because prioritized sampling introduces bias, importance-sampling weights are applied during critic training.

The intended effect is:

ordinary replay
→ many low-information experiences repeatedly sampled

PER
→ more learning updates concentrated on experiences where the critic/policy has more to learn.

The replay buffer is also shared across agents, increasing sample diversity and allowing experiences obtained by one agent to contribute to others’ learning.

9. Training and execution architecture

During centralized training, each agent provides a learned embedding to the LEM environment/platform. Attention-derived population information contributes to critic updates. Actors and critics are trained using the shared prioritized replay buffer.

During decentralized execution, the critics are no longer required. Each prosumer uses only its trained actor and its own local observation to determine actions. This is the key practical distinction between training and operation.

10. Case study setup

The case study uses a real-world Australian residential dataset and a large simulated LEM.

  • Number of prosumers: 300 residential prosumers.
  • Data source: Ausgrid residential demand and rooftop-PV dataset.
  • Weather data: Australian government open dataset.
  • Time resolution: 30 min.
  • Coordination horizon: 24 h / 48 periods.
  • Dataset horizon: one year.
  • Testing: one randomly selected day from each of 52 weeks, giving 52 test days.
  • Training: all remaining days.
  • DER heterogeneity: 80 HVAC-only; 80 HVAC+EV; 80 HVAC+PV+ES; 60 HVAC+EV+PV+ES.
  • Retail import price: Time-of-Use tariffs with summer/winter differentiation.
  • Export price: Australian Feed-in-Tariff, $0.105/kWh.
  • FS products: Regulation Raise and Regulation Lower.
  • Implementation: Python / PyTorch.
  • Hardware: 6-core 2.60 GHz Intel Core i7-10750H CPU, 32 GB RAM.
  • Optimizer: Adam.
  • Discount factor: \(\gamma=0.99\).
  • Soft-update rate: \(\tau=10^{-3}\).
  • Actor/critic: two hidden layers with 100 hidden units.
  • PER parameters: \(\beta_1=0.6\), \(\beta_2=0.4\), buffer size \(10^4\).

The paper does not report field deployment or hardware-in-the-loop validation; the study is simulation-based using real measured input data.

11. Economic value of combining local trading and FS

Four market designs are compared:

Case Energy trading FS provision
SILO Each prosumer trades independently with supplier No
SILO + FS Independent supplier trading Individual FS provision
LEM Local energy trading No
LEM + FS Local energy trading Aggregated FS provision

The average daily economic results over the 52 test days are:

Case Import cost (\() | Export revenue (\)) FS revenue (\() | Net cost (\))
SILO 2060 187 0 1873
SILO + FS 2210 212 1109 889
LEM 1459 12 0 1447
LEM + FS 1547 21 1033 493

The mechanisms behind these results are important.

Local energy trading

Local trading increases collective self-consumption. One prosumer’s excess PV can be consumed by another prosumer’s flexible DER instead of being exported at a low tariff and later replaced by high-tariff imports. This reduces both imports and exports, but the import-cost reduction dominates because the import tariff is higher than the export tariff.

Flexibility services

When FS is enabled, some DER flexibility is deliberately reserved for FS instead of being used purely to flatten the local net-load profile. This can actually increase grid imports/export in some periods. However, the additional FS revenue is sufficiently large that total net cost falls.

The key lesson is therefore:

The operating schedule with the flattest local net demand is not necessarily the economically best schedule once flexibility itself has a market value.

From the reported Table II values, the combined LEM+FS case has a net cost about 73.7% lower than SILO (derived from the paper’s reported values), demonstrating the large combined value of the two market functions in this case study.

12. Learning performance — why MAAC-PER matters

The paper compares Concurrent learning, MAAC and MAAC-PER. Centralized learning and MADDPG are also attempted but cannot be successfully executed in the 300-agent setting because of computational intractability. Parameter sharing is excluded because it assumes homogeneous agents.

Each method is trained using 10 random seeds, with 10,000 episodes per seed. Performance is evaluated on the 52-day test set every 100 episodes.

The Concurrent method remains unstable and does not converge after 10,000 episodes because 300 agents independently update their policies, continuously changing the environment seen by the others.

The reported final results are:

Case Method Net cost ($) Training time (min)
LEM Concurrent 2041 388
LEM MAAC 1475 86
LEM MAAC-PER 1447 75
LEM Theoretical benchmark 1409 —
LEM + FS Concurrent 775 445
LEM + FS MAAC 504 99
LEM + FS MAAC-PER 493 85
LEM + FS Theoretical benchmark 477 —

Relative to Concurrent learning, the authors report that MAAC-PER improves solution quality by 29.10% / 36.39% and computational performance by 80.67% / 80.90% in the LEM / LEM+FS cases.

Most importantly, MAAC-PER remains close to the idealized centralized benchmark:

  • LEM: 2.70% higher net cost than benchmark;
  • LEM + FS: 3.35% higher net cost than benchmark.

This comparison is central to the paper’s argument: a practically implementable model-free/prosumer-centric scheme loses only a small amount of economic optimality relative to a benchmark that assumes perfect models, forecasts and centralized information.

13. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — local energy trading and flexibility provision should be co-optimized

The same DER flexibility supports multiple market functions. Sequentially allocating flexibility to one market and then the other can miss better joint allocations.

Lesson 2 — minimum local energy exchange is not the same as minimum economic cost

Providing FS can make the LEM net-load profile less flat because flexibility is held back for an external service. If FS revenue is high enough, that schedule can still be economically superior.

Lesson 3 — model-free does not mean physics-free

The prosumer agent does not explicitly use DER equations when choosing actions, but the environment still enforces battery, EV and HVAC operating constraints. The physical model is moved from the decision algorithm into the environment.

Lesson 4 — multi-agent coordination needs a mechanism for non-stationarity

Independent agents make each other’s environment continually change. Attention-based centralized training gives critics enough information about the population to stabilize learning, while decentralized actors retain local execution.

Lesson 5 — DER flexibility is an opportunity cost

A kW of battery/EV/HVAC flexibility used for collective self-consumption cannot simultaneously be fully sold as external FS. Market design therefore changes the physical schedule, not just the financial settlement.

Lesson 6 — a small optimality gap may justify a much more practical architecture

The learned method is slightly more expensive than the perfect-information centralized benchmark, but avoids many of the benchmark’s information and forecasting requirements. In practical market design, implementation feasibility can be more important than achieving the mathematical optimum under unrealistic assumptions.

14. Limitations and what remains unsolved

A. Limitations explicitly stated or directly acknowledged by the paper

  1. FS activation is not modeled. Only forward trading of availability is considered; real-time utilization and utilization remuneration are excluded.
  2. Generic FS representation. The up-/down-FS formulation cannot represent special products such as dynamic frequency response or reactive-power management.
  3. Theoretical benchmark is idealized. It assumes perfect knowledge of DER operating models and accurate forecasts.
  4. Some MADRL benchmarks are computationally infeasible at 300 agents. Centralized learning and MADDPG cannot be executed successfully in the case study.

The conclusion does not provide a detailed explicit future-work list beyond the above scope boundaries.

B. Further research space visible from the formulation

These are further thoughts / possible extensions, not claims made by the authors.

  1. No explicit distribution-network constraints. Local trading is represented through aggregate energy balance and prices rather than AC/linearized power flow, voltage limits, line congestion or losses. A LEM schedule that is economically feasible is therefore not automatically distribution-network feasible.
  2. No endogenous FS market clearing or strategic bidding. FS prices are external inputs from the ESO/DSO. Prosumers learn quantities, not strategic bids into a clearing mechanism.
  3. No activation uncertainty. Selling availability creates obligations if the service is called, but the model does not represent uncertain activation energy or state-recovery requirements.
  4. Privacy is architectural rather than formally guaranteed. The method reduces direct sharing of raw local information, but the paper does not provide differential-privacy, encryption or information-leakage guarantees. Learned embeddings and shared replay structures may still deserve privacy analysis.
  5. Aggregate welfare is emphasized more than individual fairness. The main reported economic metric is the total net cost of all 300 prosumers. The distribution of benefits across heterogeneous participants and individual-rationality/participation constraints are not the central focus.
  6. EV departure feasibility is penalty-based. Required EV energy at departure is penalized rather than enforced as a hard safety constraint in the model-free formulation. Safe RL or constrained RL could provide stronger feasibility guarantees.
  7. Generalization is tested within one yearly dataset. Test days are sampled from the same one-year data source used to construct the training set. Cross-year, cross-region and structural market-change generalization are not demonstrated.
  8. Communication latency, failures and cyber-security are not modeled. These issues could matter in a distributed real-time implementation.

15. Critical reading — points worth checking before reusing the formulation

15.1 Potential reward-sign inconsistency

The Markov Game section states that each agent aims to maximize cumulative reward. However, Eq. (37) is explicitly described as the prosumer’s net cost, with import cost positive and energy/FS revenues reducing that quantity. Eq. (41) then adds a negative EV-violation penalty. Taken literally, maximizing the expression in Eq. (37) would increase cost rather than minimize it. The paper does not explain whether the implemented RL reward uses the negative of this cost. This should be verified before reproducing the method.

15.2 “Privacy-preserving” should be interpreted carefully

The paper’s privacy argument is based on avoiding direct exchange of raw observations/actions and using learned embeddings plus decentralized execution. It does not establish a formal privacy guarantee. Therefore, “privacy-preserving” here should not be interpreted as equivalent to cryptographic privacy or Differential Privacy (DP).

15.3 “Model-free” refers to agent decision-making, not the full simulator

The agent does not know its DER models, but the environment explicitly uses those models to clip/project actions and update energy and temperature states. This is a legitimate model-free RL setup, but it is important not to interpret the whole system as model-independent.

16. Research idea triggers

Idea 1 — LEM + FS + network-constrained market clearing

Extend the LEM from an aggregate energy balance to an explicit distribution network:

prosumer MADRL
→ local energy + FS bids
→ network-constrained clearing / DLMP
→ voltage and line limits.

This would test whether economically attractive flexibility schedules remain physically deliverable.

Idea 2 — forward FS availability + uncertain real-time activation

Add a second stage for actual FS activation. The learning problem would need to reserve sufficient state-of-charge/thermal margins under uncertain call probabilities, creating a natural stochastic or distributionally robust extension.

Idea 3 — safe/constrained MADRL for hard service guarantees

Replace penalty-only handling of critical constraints, especially EV departure energy, with Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), safe RL or shielded/projection-based methods. This could provide explicit constraint-violation guarantees.

Idea 4 — fairness-aware local energy and flexibility market

The current case study mainly optimizes aggregate net cost. A natural extension is to combine system efficiency with benefit allocation, individual rationality or fairness metrics so that no subgroup consistently provides flexibility without adequate compensation.

Idea 5 — adaptive / continual MADRL under market and population changes

Test structural changes such as new prosumers joining/leaving, DER portfolio changes, tariff redesign, FS-price regime shifts or changing user comfort preferences. This would move from stationary offline training toward continual market adaptation.

Idea 6 — privacy-quantified MARL

Combine MAAC-style compressed coordination with formal privacy mechanisms such as DP, federated learning or secure aggregation, and explicitly quantify the trade-off between privacy loss, communication burden and market efficiency.

Idea 7 — multi-market flexibility stacking

Extend the two-function LEM to simultaneous participation in local energy, congestion management, balancing, reserve and possibly carbon/flexibility markets. The core question becomes how to allocate one physical unit of DER flexibility among competing revenue streams with different time scales and activation risks.

注记[P032] Hupez et al. (2023) — Pricing Electricity in Residential Communities Using Game-Theoretical Billings

Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, Vol. 14, No. 2, March 2023, pp. 1621–1631
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2022.3206912
Main topics: residential energy communities; electricity billing; fairness; game theory; Nash equilibrium; Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) mechanism; distributed optimization; demand-side management; prosumer flexibility; energy storage; photovoltaic generation; supplier tariffs

Quick takeaway

This paper asks a deceptively simple but important question: if a residential community is coordinated so that the total electricity cost is reduced, how should that cost be divided among individual prosumers? The issue is difficult because prosumers share the same low-voltage network, their actions jointly determine nonlinear grid costs, and their DER portfolios differ substantially. A billing rule therefore does more than split a bill: it changes incentives, strategic behavior, flexibility provision, and ultimately the operating point of the whole community.

The authors compare three game-theoretical billing schemes for day-ahead scheduling in a liberalized electricity market where each prosumer may choose its own supplier and may own photovoltaic (PV), storage (ST), electric vehicles (EV), and flexible appliances such as heat pumps (HP). Two schemes use daily proportional billing and reach the social optimum, while the third uses continuous proportional billing and gives stronger individual bargaining/decision incentives at the price of a small efficiency loss.

The central lesson is that fairness is not one-dimensional. One billing can be system-efficient but weak in individual empowerment; another can better reward flexibility and individual behavior but permit strategic deviations from the social optimum. In the representative case study, continuous proportional billing has a mean daily inefficiency of only 1.97%, while better exposing individuals to the consequences of their own timing and supplier choices.

1. Problem addressed — optimal community operation does not automatically imply fair individual bills

Residential prosumers increasingly share local infrastructure while owning heterogeneous Distributed Energy Resources (DERs). They may have PV generation, batteries, EVs, heat pumps, and other flexible loads. Their actions are interdependent because all of them use the same low-voltage network.

A central or distributed scheduling mechanism can reduce the aggregate community cost, but this does not answer the allocation question:

If the community as a whole saves money, who should pay how much?

This matters because different users contribute differently to the community outcome. A prosumer with storage may reduce peaks and grid costs. A PV owner may reduce imports but can also create reverse flows. A flexible user may shift demand to beneficial hours. Another consumer may contribute very little flexibility but still benefit from the collective schedule.

Therefore, the paper studies the interaction between:

  • system efficiency — minimizing the total commodity and grid cost;
  • fairness / cost allocation — how the total cost is distributed among participants;
  • individual empowerment — whether a prosumer can improve its own bill through useful behavior;
  • tractability — whether the billing rule and equilibrium can be computed in a realistic distributed setting.

2. Why existing approaches are not enough

The authors identify several gaps in previous local-market and demand-side-management studies.

First, many market designs focus on local spot markets or peer-to-peer mechanisms, while network costs are difficult to allocate fairly. Distribution Locational Marginal Prices (DLMPs) can reflect physical constraints, but their location-dependent prices may raise fairness concerns, and the paper instead explores billing rules that pass through the actual incurred commodity and grid costs.

Second, much previous demand-side-management literature assumes a single utility and does not represent a liberalized market in which different households can contract different suppliers. In the paper, each supplier can offer a different time-varying commodity tariff, so supplier choice itself affects the bill.

Third, previous fairness studies are often limited to one billing mechanism or one fairness dimension. The authors argue that the outcome depends strongly on the prosumer profile — especially PV ownership and flexibility — so different billing mechanisms need to be compared systematically under the same physical and economic setting.

Finally, the authors extend earlier work by explicitly including energy storage and modern flexible-load profiles.

3. Residential community and cost architecture

The community consists of all prosumers connected behind the same low-voltage transformer. Each prosumer may select a different electricity supplier but shares the same distribution infrastructure with the others.

For prosumer \(n\), the net load is

\[ \mathbf l_n = \mathbf d_n + \mathbf x_n + \mathbf s_n, \]

where:

  • \(\mathbf d_n\) is the uncontrollable baseload minus PV generation;
  • \(\mathbf x_n\) is the flexible-appliance schedule;
  • \(\mathbf s_n\) is the storage charging/discharging schedule.

The paper separates electricity costs into two parts.

3.1 Commodity cost

Each prosumer is contracted with a supplier. Supplier \(i\) charges time-varying commodity price \(\gamma^t_{com,i}\) for positive net imports:

\[ C^t_{supp,i}(l_n^t)=\gamma^t_{com,i}l_n^{t+}\tau. \]

A notable assumption is that suppliers do not buy back exports from prosumers; only positive net load is billed. The paper motivates this by the near-zero marginal generation cost of behind-the-meter renewable generation.

3.2 Grid cost

All prosumers jointly determine the aggregate network loading

\[ L^t=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}l_n^t. \]

The grid cost is modeled as a quadratic function:

\[ C^t_{grid}=\gamma_{grid}(L^t\tau)^2. \]

This quadratic form represents the nonlinear dependence of network-related costs on aggregate flow and, crucially, creates interdependence: one household’s schedule changes the cost faced by the whole community.

The model does not include explicit branch flows, voltage limits, or AC power flow. The community is represented as a single entity behind one transformer.

4. Three billing philosophies

The paper compares three methods. They are not merely accounting rules: each changes the incentives inside the scheduling game.

4.1 Net-load proportional billing (Net)

The first method distributes the optimized daily community bill according to a fixed weight based on each prosumer’s minimum possible cumulative positive net load \(L_n^*\):

\[ b_n^{Net} = \frac{L_n^*}{\sum_m L_m^*}f(\Lambda). \]

Using the minimum possible positive net load rather than the realized load prevents a prosumer from strategically manipulating the distribution key after the scheduling decisions are made.

Interpretation: this is the most egalitarian and computationally simple option, but it weakly rewards individual flexibility. Two users with very different temporal behavior can face the same average price if their allocation weights are similar.

4.2 Marginal-cost / VCG billing (VCG)

The second daily scheme uses a normalized Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) idea. The weight of prosumer \(n\) is its marginal contribution to the optimal community cost:

\[ w_n=C^*_{\mathcal N}-C^*_{\mathcal N\setminus\{n\}}. \]

Hence,

\[ b_n^{VCG} = \frac{C^*_{\mathcal N}-C^*_{\mathcal N\setminus\{n\}}} {\sum_m\left(C^*_{\mathcal N}-C^*_{\mathcal N\setminus\{m\}}\right)} f(\Lambda). \]

The logic is: how much does the community outcome change because this participant is present? Participants that contribute useful flexibility can therefore obtain more favorable cost allocation.

The method achieves the social optimum and has a truthful-strategy interpretation, but it is computationally expensive because it requires solving the full optimization problem plus one counterfactual problem for each participant, i.e., \(N+1\) optimization problems.

4.3 Continuous proportional billing (CP)

The third method allocates costs at every time slot rather than once over the whole day:

\[ b_n^{CP} = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} \left( \gamma^t_{com,i}l_n^{t+}\tau + \gamma_{grid}l_n^tL^t\tau^2 \right). \]

This billing directly exposes each prosumer to:

  • the commodity price of its own contracted supplier;
  • its own time-varying net load;
  • the aggregate community load at the same time.

Therefore, individual behavior is more visible in the final bill. The trade-off is that agents can strategically react to the billing formula, so the resulting Nash equilibrium is not guaranteed to coincide with the social optimum.

5. Flexible resources — what creates bargaining power?

The paper models four important household characteristics:

  • PV: treated as negative non-flexible load;
  • ST: energy storage that can charge in cheap periods or absorb PV surplus;
  • EV: partially flexible load with allowed charging windows and energy requirements;
  • HP: heat pump, simplified as a fully flexible load for the case study.

Storage is modeled with energy capacity, charging/discharging efficiency, leakage, and power limits. Flexible appliances must satisfy their required daily energy while operating inside user-permitted time windows.

The main conceptual point is that flexibility changes both physical cost and bargaining position. A flexible user can avoid expensive aggregate peaks and shift consumption toward cheaper commodity periods, while a PV owner without flexibility may reduce its own imports but still produce network flows that are not beneficial to the community under every billing rule.

6. Game formulation — every prosumer minimizes its own bill

The day-ahead scheduling problem is formulated as a non-cooperative game. Each prosumer is a player that chooses its flexible-load and storage schedule \(\Lambda_n\) while treating the others’ schedules \(\Lambda_{-n}\) as given:

\[ \min_{\Lambda_n} \; b_n(\Lambda_n,\Lambda_{-n}) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad \Lambda_n\in\Omega_n. \]

A Nash equilibrium is reached when no prosumer can reduce its own bill by changing its schedule unilaterally.

The paper establishes that the game has a non-empty, compact Nash-equilibrium set under the considered convex formulation, and that all Nash equilibria yield the same objective-function values.

7. Distributed equilibrium computation

The two billing classes require different algorithms.

7.1 Daily proportional billing — asynchronous best response

For Net and VCG billing, minimizing each prosumer’s bill also drives the cumulative community cost downward. Therefore, the Nash equilibrium corresponds to the minimum of the aggregate cost function.

The paper uses an asynchronous best-response algorithm: at selected iterations, each participant optimizes its own schedule given the current schedules of all others.

7.2 Continuous proportional billing — proximal decomposition

Pure best response is not sufficient for CP because an individual reduction of \(b_n^{CP}\) does not necessarily reduce the total community cost. The authors therefore use a proximal decomposition algorithm, adding a regularization term that stabilizes the iterative game:

\[ \min_{\Lambda_n} \left[ b_n(\Lambda_n,\Lambda_{-n}) +\frac{\kappa}{2}\|\Lambda_n-\bar\Lambda_n\|^2 \right]. \]

Both distributed approaches require only aggregate-load information to be exchanged. The paper therefore describes them as privacy-preserving in the sense that detailed individual schedules do not need to be disclosed to a central third party.

The paper does not provide a formal privacy guarantee such as differential privacy or cryptographic protection.

8. Why the billing rules produce different behavior

The qualitative comparison in Fig. 2 is particularly useful because it shows that the same physical prosumer can be rewarded very differently depending on the billing philosophy.

The four illustrative comparisons consider a reference consumer versus a prosumer with:

  1. PV only;
  2. EV + HP + ST;
  3. PV + EV + HP + ST;
  4. the same portfolio as Case 3 but with a different supplier tariff.

Important observations are:

  • PV alone does not automatically obtain favorable treatment under VCG. Because PV by itself is not flexible, the VCG rule may not interpret it as a strong contributor to reducing the optimized community cost.
  • Flexible DERs are rewarded by discriminative billings. EV, HP, and storage can shift energy away from costly periods and therefore reduce the prosumer’s effective price under VCG and CP.
  • PV plus flexibility performs better than PV alone, because storage/flexible demand can absorb surplus generation and avoid adverse network effects.
  • Supplier choice matters strongly under CP, because commodity and grid costs are explicitly separated at each time step. A tariff that matches the prosumer’s load/PV profile can materially lower its bill.

9. Case study setting

The quantitative benchmark is based on residential data from the Pecan Street project.

Key settings are:

  • 50 residential prosumers in the representative community case study;
  • load profiles sampled from the Pecan Street residential dataset;
  • PV, ST, EV, and HP assigned in different combinations;
  • two suppliers with different cheaper-day / cheaper-night tariff structures;
  • 20 highest-PV days and 20 lowest-PV days analyzed separately;
  • deterministic day-ahead scheduling;
  • global optimum used as the efficiency benchmark;
  • the paper does not report a commercial solver in the main text for the comparative study;
  • full device parameters are delegated to an online companion source cited by the paper.

The socially optimal mean price is reported as:

  • 15.0 c€/kWh for high-PV days;
  • 22.4 c€/kWh for low-PV days.

10. Main findings

10.1 Billing discrimination matters mainly when DER interactions are strong

On low-PV days, the three billing methods discriminate only weakly among different prosumer profiles. With little local generation, added flexible demand can still increase imports, so the benefit of flexibility is comparatively limited.

On high-PV days, the differences become much larger because flexibility can absorb local PV surplus and mitigate reverse-flow-related grid cost. The billing rule therefore strongly affects who captures this value.

For high-PV days, Table II reports the following relative changes in mean price:

  • under VCG, HP ownership: -7.0%; ST ownership: -11.3%; all considered DERs: -8.5%;
  • under CP, PV ownership: -4.6%; HP ownership: -6.1%; ST ownership: -6.7%; all considered DERs: -3.9%.

A striking result is that PV ownership alone produces a lower mean price only under CP in the high-PV comparison. Under VCG, the PV owner’s relative price is slightly higher (+0.2%), because VCG rewards contribution to the optimized community outcome rather than PV ownership per se.

10.2 Continuous proportional billing sacrifices little efficiency

The paper measures CP inefficiency as

\[ \frac{\sum_n b_n^{CP}-C^*_{\mathcal N}}{C^*_{\mathcal N}}. \]

The key quantitative result is:

  • mean daily inefficiency over the full dataset: 1.97%;
  • with no PV generation, inefficiency is below 0.01% under the tested conditions;
  • the larger inefficiencies appear mainly on high-PV days.

Why? Under CP, the grid-cost component is strategically sensitive. PV owners can increase self-consumption just enough to retain a favorable individual position relative to the aggregate load, creating bargaining power but moving the system away from the global optimum.

10.3 Tariff design changes both system cost and bargaining power

The baseline supplier design yields mean prices of 15.0 c€/kWh on high-PV days and 22.4 c€/kWh on low-PV days. When the day/night price gap is reduced, the corresponding values become 15.7 / 21.6 c€/kWh; under a flat tariff they become 16.8 / 21.4 c€/kWh.

The result shows that a tariff cannot be evaluated independently from the DER mix: making night energy more expensive hurts high-PV-day performance, while reduced daytime prices can help low-PV days.

11. Efficiency, empowerment and tractability — no billing dominates on every dimension

The paper’s overall comparison can be summarized as follows:

Billing System efficiency Individual empowerment Computational tractability
Net Social optimum Weak / neutral Strong
VCG Social optimum Rewards contribution Moderate-to-low due to \(N+1\) solves
CP Slightly inefficient Strong individual responsiveness Moderate

This is the key conceptual result of the paper: billing design is a multi-objective mechanism-design problem. There is no universally “fairest” scheme unless fairness itself is defined first.

12. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — minimum total cost is not the same problem as fair cost allocation

The community can have a unique or near-unique aggregate optimum while very different billing rules assign that outcome’s benefits and burdens differently. Optimization and allocation should therefore be analyzed separately.

Lesson 2 — fairness has competing interpretations

A Net rule emphasizes equal treatment according to a fixed consumption-related key. VCG emphasizes marginal contribution to the community. CP emphasizes individual agency and timing-sensitive responsibility. These are different notions of fairness rather than different numerical implementations of the same concept.

Lesson 3 — flexibility is economically valuable only if the billing rule recognizes it

A user may own technically flexible DERs, but a billing scheme that does not link the final payment to useful flexibility can provide little incentive to expose that flexibility to the community.

Lesson 4 — PV generation and flexibility are not equivalent

PV can reduce imports but is not dispatchable in the paper’s model. VCG can therefore value storage or flexible demand more strongly than PV alone, especially when the question is “who helped the community reduce the optimized total cost?”

Lesson 5 — supplier tariffs and local network costs interact

In a liberalized setting, users can contract different suppliers, but all still share the same physical grid. A good individual commodity tariff can therefore conflict with network-efficient scheduling, depending on the billing mechanism.

Lesson 6 — distributed does not automatically mean formally private

The algorithms reduce information sharing by requiring mainly aggregate-load information, but the paper does not establish a formal privacy guarantee.

13. Limitations / what remains unsolved

A. Limitations and future work explicitly stated by the authors

  • The current community is effectively represented behind a common transformer rather than through detailed meshed-network power flow.
  • The authors identify partially or fully meshed networks as an important extension.
  • Adding explicit power-flow constraints would introduce shared constraints and turn the problem into a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem (GNEP).
  • The paper notes that a more cooperative framework with mutualized excess PV/community resources could yield more representative cost distributions, but this is beyond its scope.

B. Further research space visible from the model

  • Deterministic day-ahead setting: uncertainty in PV, demand, prices, EV availability, and user behavior is not explicitly modeled.
  • Simplified network representation: the quadratic aggregate grid cost is not a substitute for branch-level congestion, voltage constraints, or losses from AC power flow.
  • No export remuneration: suppliers are assumed not to buy prosumer exports, which may not fit all regulatory environments.
  • Supplier choice is exogenous: prosumers are assigned/assumed to select suppliers rather than jointly optimizing supplier contract and operational schedule.
  • Storage degradation is omitted: cycling cost may materially change which users should be rewarded for flexibility.
  • Simplified appliance representation: the model avoids fixed-cycle appliances requiring binary variables; HP is treated as fully flexible in the illustrative analysis.
  • No formal privacy guarantee: only aggregate information exchange is required, but information leakage is not quantified.
  • Fairness is assessed economically, not behaviorally: long-term acceptance, participation, and strategic entry/exit are not modeled.
  • Static community membership: DER investment and flexibility consent are treated as given rather than endogenous responses to billing design.

14. Critical reading

  1. The network-cost model is intentionally stylized. The quadratic aggregate-load term is useful for studying billing incentives, but the paper’s claims about “grid cost” should not be interpreted as a full distribution-network feasibility model.

  2. “Privacy-preserving” should be interpreted cautiously. The algorithms avoid sharing detailed individual schedules and do not rely on a third-party centralized optimizer, but there is no differential-privacy, encryption, or information-theoretic privacy analysis.

  3. VCG fairness depends on the chosen counterfactual and cost model. The paper itself stresses that VCG is not intrinsically fair in every context; it rewards marginal contribution according to the modeled community objective.

  4. There appears to be a wording inconsistency around empowerment in Section IV-E. Table IV assigns the strongest empowerment rating (“++”) to continuous proportional billing and only “+” to VCG, which is consistent with the surrounding discussion that CP gives prosumers more negotiation power. However, one sentence states that marginal cost billing has the best potential for mobilizing individual efforts. This appears inconsistent with Table IV and nearby text, so it should not be silently reconciled.

  5. The CP inefficiency is highly scenario-dependent. The reported mean value of 1.97% is convincing for the tested dataset, but it increases on high-PV days and is not a theoretical universal upper bound.

15. Research idea triggers

Idea 1 — Network-constrained game-theoretical billing

Extend the single-transformer model to an explicit radial or meshed distribution network:

billing rule + AC/linearized power flow + voltage/congestion constraints → GNEP.

This would connect fairness directly to physical network feasibility rather than a quadratic proxy cost.

Idea 2 — Distributionally robust or stochastic billing games

Replace deterministic day-ahead inputs with uncertain PV, demand, EV availability, and prices. A natural direction is:

billing mechanism + stochastic/robust/DRO scheduling + fairness under uncertainty.

The key research question becomes whether a billing scheme remains fair when participants contribute differently to forecast risk.

Idea 3 — Dynamic fairness over repeated days

The current analysis is day-by-day. In practice, one household may contribute flexibility today and another tomorrow. A repeated-game or rolling-horizon design could enforce inter-temporal fairness instead of requiring every single day to be fair in isolation.

Idea 4 — Endogenous flexibility participation

Model the user’s willingness to expose EV, storage, or thermal flexibility as a decision. This would test the paper’s qualitative hypothesis that stronger empowerment can induce more flexibility and potentially offset a small efficiency loss.

Idea 5 — Joint tariff selection and scheduling

The paper shows supplier choice matters but treats it outside the main scheduling game. A richer model could jointly optimize:

supplier contract + DER schedule + community billing + network cost.

Idea 6 — Formal privacy-preserving distributed billing

Combine the distributed game with differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, or federated optimization and quantify the trade-off:

privacy protection ↔︎ billing accuracy ↔︎ convergence ↔︎ efficiency.

Idea 7 — Fairness with degradation and opportunity costs

For batteries and EVs, include degradation and user inconvenience so that the “marginal contribution” reflects the private cost of providing flexibility, not only the system benefit.

16. Position in the broader literature map

This paper sits at the intersection of energy communities, demand-side flexibility, mechanism design, and distributed game theory. Compared with papers that focus mainly on finding the least-cost operating schedule, its distinctive question is:

Once a community has a shared physical cost, how should individual payments be designed so that efficiency, fairness, and behavioral incentives remain aligned?

This makes it particularly useful as a bridge between technical DER scheduling and market-design studies on benefit allocation, P2P trading, local tariffs, and fairness.

Problem-map tags: cost allocation · billing fairness · prosumer incentives · community energy management · network cost allocation · Nash equilibrium · VCG mechanism · distributed optimization · flexibility valuation · supplier choice · strategic behavior · social optimum · privacy · network constraints

注记[P033] ZareiJeliani et al. (2026) — Real-Time AI-Driven Energy and Flexibility Management for a Technical Virtual Power Plant

Journal: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, Vol. 17, No. 4, July 2026, pp. 2810–2821
DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2026.3661242
Main topics: technical virtual power plant (TVPP); real-time energy market; flexibility market; flexible ramping; distributed energy resources (DERs); multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL); Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO); Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE); transfer learning; linear programming (LP); CNN-LSTM forecasting; electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs); energy storage systems (ESSs); distribution network constraints

Quick takeaway

This paper studies how a Technical Virtual Power Plant (TVPP) can jointly manage energy and flexibility in real time while respecting distribution-network constraints. The TVPP aggregates photovoltaic (PV) generation, wind turbines (WTs), distributed generators (DGs), Energy Storage Systems (ESSs), and Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCSs), and participates in both the real-time energy market and upward/downward flexibility markets at a 5-minute resolution.

The paper combines three ideas. First, a Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) model predicts short-term flexibility requirements using quantile forecasts of net load. Second, a hybrid optimization framework decomposes the original Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) scheduling problem: EVCS and ESS decisions, including the discrete charging/discharging choices, are handled by Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), while the remaining system-level decisions and network constraints are handled by an LP model. Third, single-agent Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policies are pre-trained and transferred to the multi-agent environment to accelerate training and improve stability.

The main methodological message is that the paper does not replace mathematical optimization with end-to-end reinforcement learning. Instead, it deliberately separates adaptive sequential decisions from hard system constraints. RL handles the most dynamic and combinatorial parts, while LP supplies feasibility-oriented system feedback. In the reported tests on the IEEE 33-bus system, the proposed method achieves higher normalized profit than the paper’s intra-hourly mathematical-optimization benchmark and supports instantaneous online decisions after training.

1. Problem addressed — real-time flexibility management is both a forecasting and coordination problem

The TVPP participates in a real-time market where renewable generation, electricity prices, EV availability, loads, and flexibility requirements change rapidly. The central operational problem is therefore not only to schedule energy, but also to maintain enough upward flexibility (UF) and downward flexibility (DF) to respond to short-term net-load changes.

Too little flexibility can cause ramp shortages, power-balance problems, or stronger reliance on regulation services. Too much flexibility is also costly because capacity must be reserved instead of being used for energy production, charging, or other profitable purposes. Therefore, the TVPP must answer two coupled questions:

  1. How much flexibility will the system need in the next short interval?
  2. How should heterogeneous DERs be scheduled so that the TVPP earns market revenue while retaining sufficient deliverable flexibility and respecting network constraints?

The problem is particularly difficult at a 5-minute time scale because conventional optimization must repeatedly solve a large problem containing binary charging/discharging variables, inter-temporal SOC dynamics, ramp constraints, market transactions, and distribution-network limits.

2. Why existing approaches are not enough

The paper identifies limitations on both sides of the traditional solution spectrum.

2.1 Mathematical optimization

Mathematical programming can explicitly represent physical constraints and produce feasible schedules, but the authors argue that large real-time problems become difficult when they contain many DERs, binary operating decisions, uncertainty, and short decision intervals. A monolithic MILP is therefore viewed as insufficiently adaptive and potentially difficult to scale.

2.2 Pure reinforcement learning

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can learn adaptive policies for uncertain and sequential environments, but previous RL-based energy-management studies can suffer from:

  • high-dimensional state/action spaces;
  • slow or unstable training;
  • difficulty coordinating multiple DERs;
  • lack of explicit feasibility guarantees for network and operational constraints.

The paper’s response is therefore a hybrid architecture rather than a purely model-based or purely learning-based solution.

2.3 Flexibility forecasting

The paper also argues that conventional statistical methods may not capture the nonlinear and sequential relationships among renewable production, demand, weather, and net-load uncertainty. This motivates a data-driven CNN-LSTM quantile model for flexibility-requirement prediction.

3. TVPP market and resource architecture

The TVPP aggregates several types of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs):

  • PV panels;
  • wind turbines;
  • dispatchable DGs;
  • ESSs;
  • EVCSs;
  • fixed loads.

It participates in two coupled markets:

  • real-time energy market, through buying and selling active power;
  • flexibility market, through selling upward and downward flexibility.

The paper distinguishes a TVPP from a purely commercial VPP by explicitly incorporating technical network constraints, including nodal power balance, voltage limits, and line-loading limits.

The objective for each interval maximizes TVPP profit from energy and flexibility transactions while accounting for DG production/flexibility costs, renewable purchases, and load-related revenues.

A simplified representation is:

\[ \max \; \text{Energy-market profit} + \text{Flexibility revenue} + \text{Load revenue} - \text{renewable purchase cost} - \text{DG operating and flexibility costs}. \]

The important point is that energy and flexibility are co-optimized: the amount of flexibility a device can sell depends on its baseline energy schedule.

4. Forecasting upward and downward flexibility requirements

The paper derives flexibility requirements from predicted net-load movement plus forecast uncertainty.

For interval \(i\), upward flexibility is:

\[ X_i^U = \max\left[(L^{pred}_{i+1}+\sigma^U_{i+1})-L^{pred}_i,0\right], \]

and downward flexibility is:

\[ X_i^D = \max\left[L^{pred}_i-(L^{pred}_{i+1}-\sigma^D_{i+1}),0\right]. \]

Here:

  • \(L^{pred}\) is predicted net load;
  • \(\sigma^U\) and \(\sigma^D\) are upward/downward uncertainty margins;
  • \(X^U\) and \(X^D\) become the flexibility requirements used by the scheduling framework.

The interpretation is straightforward: if the next interval may have a higher-than-expected net load, the system needs enough upward capability; if it may have a lower-than-expected net load, it needs enough downward capability.

4.1 CNN-LSTM quantile forecasting

The CNN-LSTM predicts the 0.025, 0.5, and 0.975 quantiles of net-load components. The median gives the central forecast, while the distance to the lower and upper quantiles produces the uncertainty margins used in the flexibility equations.

The quantile loss is:

\[ QL(\hat y,y;\tau)= \begin{cases} \tau(y-\hat y), & y\ge \hat y,\\ (\tau-1)(y-\hat y), & y<\hat y. \end{cases} \]

The paper therefore translates forecast uncertainty directly into a market-relevant flexibility requirement, rather than forecasting flexibility prices or DER actions directly.

5. DER flexibility models — energy schedule determines available reserve

5.1 EVCS flexibility

Each EV can charge, idle, or discharge. SOC evolves according to:

\[ SOC_{EV,k}(t)=SOC_{EV,k}(t-1) +\frac{\Delta t}{C_k} \left(P_{charge,k}(t)-P_{discharge,k}(t)\right). \]

The model prevents simultaneous charging and discharging and enforces charging/discharging power limits.

The important flexibility logic is that an EV’s ability to provide UF or DF depends on its current baseline charging/discharging point and remaining power/SOC headroom. The paper also evaluates SOC trajectories under hypothetical flexibility activation to ensure that offered flexibility does not violate feasible SOC ranges.

A departure-SOC target represents customer service quality. This creates an important rebound mechanism: if EV charging is postponed to provide flexibility, the missing energy must still be recovered before departure.

5.2 ESS flexibility

The ESS uses an analogous SOC model. Its upward and downward flexibility are bounded by both:

  • charging/discharging power headroom;
  • SOC headroom under the potential flexibility action.

5.3 DG flexibility

DG output is constrained by capacity and inter-temporal ramping limits. Its flexibility is limited by both ramp capability and remaining upward/downward generation margin.

6. Hybrid MAPPO-LP decomposition — RL handles adaptive discrete decisions, LP enforces system-level coordination

The core framework is summarized in Fig. 2.

The original scheduling formulation is described as an MILP. The authors decompose it as follows:

RL/MAPPO subproblem
Handles EVCS and ESS decision variables, including binary/discrete charging and discharging behavior.

LP subproblem
Handles the remaining system-level operation, including market transactions, DG dispatch, flexibility balance, and network constraints after the RL decisions are fixed.

The two components are not independent. The RL actions are passed into the LP, and the LP returns feasibility and objective information to the learning process. The authors therefore describe the method as a constraint-aware cooperative optimization framework.

This architecture is central to the paper’s contribution:

Instead of encoding every physical constraint inside a reward function, the method leaves difficult system-wide feasibility checks to mathematical optimization.

7. MAPPO with Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE)

The EVCS and ESS are modeled as separate RL agents. The final cooperative learner uses Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) under Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE).

During training:

  • each EVCS/ESS actor produces local actions;
  • a shared centralized critic evaluates their joint behavior;
  • the mathematical optimization layer checks system-wide feasibility/performance;
  • LP feedback is embedded in the global reward.

During online execution:

  • the trained actors make decisions using their local observations;
  • the paper describes the online decisions as instantaneous;
  • the centralized critic is not required for decentralized action selection.

The global reward is defined as:

\[ R_{global}(t) =\alpha R_{EVCS}(t) +\beta R_{ESS}(t) +\gamma C_{feedback}(t). \]

The LP feedback is:

\[ C_{feedback}(t)= \begin{cases} \epsilon-C_{Obj}(t), & \text{if feasible},\\ -\delta-C_{Obj}(t), & \text{if infeasible}. \end{cases} \]

Thus the agents are rewarded not only for their local operating objectives, but also for producing actions that are compatible with the global optimization problem.

8. PPO pre-training and transfer learning

Training a multi-agent policy from scratch can be unstable and slow. The paper therefore first trains two single-agent PPO policies:

  • one for EVCS operation;
  • one for ESS operation.

These pretrained actor parameters are then transferred to the MAPPO framework and fine-tuned jointly. All layers remain trainable during the multi-agent stage.

The intended logic is:

simple single-agent environment
→ learn basic charging/discharging behavior
→ transfer actor parameters
→ cooperative multi-agent fine-tuning
→ faster/stabler convergence.

This is an important practical design choice because the multi-agent learner does not need to discover elementary ESS/EV behavior from random initialization.

9. State, action, and reward design

9.1 EVCS state

The EVCS state includes:

  • current time;
  • renewable generation;
  • current market price;
  • next-period predicted price;
  • average predicted future price over a selected window;
  • EV SOC;
  • remaining time to departure;
  • deviation from target departure SOC;
  • upward and downward system flexibility requirements.

9.2 ESS state

The ESS state uses the same market/renewable/flexibility information but replaces EV-specific departure variables with ESS SOC.

9.3 Actions

For each EV or ESS, the action set is discrete:

\[ \{-P_{max},0,+P_{max}\}, \]

representing discharging, idling, or charging.

9.4 Reward structure

Local rewards combine:

  • energy-arbitrage incentives based on current and predicted prices;
  • rewards/penalties for flexibility contribution;
  • SOC-limit penalties;
  • flexibility-related SOC feasibility penalties;
  • for EVs, a strong departure-SOC penalty.

The reward coefficients are not analytically derived. The authors state that they were selected through iterative sensitivity analysis to obtain stable convergence and comparable gradient magnitudes across objectives.

10. Distribution-network feasibility

The model incorporates a DistFlow-based network representation. The paper explicitly refers to:

  • nodal active-power balance;
  • reactive-power relations;
  • voltage bounds \(V_{min}\le V_i(t)\le V_{max}\);
  • line-loading limits.

This is an important difference from many VPP or aggregator papers that optimize only an aggregate power balance. Here, market actions are intended to remain feasible within the physical distribution network.

However, several detailed DistFlow expressions are referred back to the authors’ previous work rather than fully reproduced in this paper.

11. Case study and training setup

The main test system is the IEEE 33-bus distribution network.

Data

  • weather: temperature, wind speed, and solar radiation;
  • power-system time series: fixed load, market price, WT output, and PV output;
  • Austrian data covering 2015–2018;
  • EV behavior from the ACN dataset;
  • original 15-minute data are stated to be refined to 5-minute resolution;
  • real-time energy/flexibility transactions use 5-minute intervals.

Flexibility forecasting model

CNN-LSTM architecture:

  • Conv1D: 5 filters, kernel size 5, ReLU;
  • MaxPooling1D: pool size 2;
  • LSTM: 20 units, tanh;
  • Dense output layer;
  • quantiles: 0.025, 0.5, 0.975;
  • trained using three years of data.

Reported test metrics for net-load prediction are:

Prediction RMSE \(R^2\) MAE MAPE
Mean 46.0923 0.9942 32.1877 1.84%
Lower boundary 57.6923 0.9909 45.7101 2.67%
Upper boundary 60.6352 0.9900 47.5235 2.87%

RL dataset and training split

  • 44-day dataset for the RL experiments;
  • 34 days training;
  • 10 days testing;
  • the detailed operating example uses Day 41.

PPO pre-training

  • two hidden layers with 64 neurons each;
  • learning rate: \(3\times10^{-4}\);
  • discount factor: \(\gamma=0.99\);
  • GAE parameter: \(\lambda=0.95\);
  • batch size: 64;
  • n-steps: 288;
  • entropy coefficient: 0.01.

MAPPO fine-tuning

  • centralized critic: three hidden layers, 256 neurons each;
  • learning rate: \(1\times10^{-5}\);
  • \(\gamma=0.99\);
  • \(\lambda=0.95\);
  • entropy coefficient: 0.01;
  • global reward weights reported as \(\alpha=0.35\), \(\beta=0.35\), \(\gamma=1\), \(\delta=500\), and \(\epsilon=5\).

Software

  • Python;
  • PyTorch for DL/DRL;
  • PuLP with CBC solver for LP optimization.

12. Main findings

12.1 Flexibility forecasting is accurate on the reported test data

The quantile CNN-LSTM achieves \(R^2\) values close to 0.99 for the mean, lower, and upper net-load boundaries. The median and uncertainty bounds are then converted directly into UF/DF requirements.

The main value of this forecasting stage is therefore not merely predicting net load; it produces the uncertainty margins that determine how much flexibility the TVPP should retain.

12.2 PPO pre-training provides stable initial policies

The individual EVCS and ESS reward trajectories increase rapidly at the beginning and then stabilize. These policies are used to initialize the MAPPO actors rather than starting the cooperative learner from random policies.

12.3 LP feedback helps cooperative training recover from early constraint violations

The MAPPO global reward initially drops when the pretrained single-agent policies are first coupled. The paper attributes this to early infeasibility and coordination conflicts. The reward later recovers and stabilizes as the agents adapt to the shared critic and LP feedback.

The authors report smoother convergence and higher steady-state reward than independently trained PPO controllers under the same environment.

12.4 EVCS and ESS supply much of the short-term flexibility

On the detailed test day, EVs and ESSs provide much of the required upward/downward flexibility through charging/discharging adjustments, while DGs become important during intervals with attractive flexibility prices.

This illustrates an important flexibility principle: energy-limited assets can provide rapid short-term flexibility, while dispatchable generation supplies additional capacity when market signals justify it.

12.5 Proposed method reports 10%–35% higher normalized profit than the mathematical-optimization benchmark

Across test Days 35–44, the proposed method is reported to achieve approximately 10%–35% higher system profit, with the authors attributing the improvement mainly to more effective exploitation of EV and ESS flexibility.

The paper normalizes the profit values and states that objective-function components were balanced to provide consistent comparisons.

12.6 Computational comparison

Table II reports:

Method Training time Online decision time
PPO (EVCS) 1.34 s/episode Instantly
PPO (ESS) 0.3 s/episode Instantly
Proposed MAPPO-LP 12.93 s/episode Instantly
MILP N/A 0.12 s/interval

The authors argue that the proposed method is attractive for dynamic real-time operation because most computation is shifted to offline training and the learned actors can produce immediate decisions online.

13. What this paper teaches

Lesson 1 — flexibility forecasting and flexibility dispatch are two distinct problems

Before an aggregator can sell flexibility, it must determine how much flexibility is actually needed. The paper explicitly connects probabilistic net-load forecasting to the later market and dispatch problem.

Lesson 2 — energy schedules define flexibility headroom

An ESS, EV, or DG does not have a fixed flexibility value. Its available UF/DF depends on its current operating point, SOC, power limits, and future obligations. Therefore, energy and flexibility should be co-optimized.

Lesson 3 — hybrid RL + optimization can separate adaptation from feasibility

The paper’s most transferable methodological idea is to let RL learn uncertain sequential behavior while leaving network and system-wide constraints to mathematical optimization. This can be more reliable than forcing every constraint into a reward function.

Lesson 4 — pre-training is useful when multi-agent learning contains recognizable single-agent subproblems

EVCS and ESS control can first be learned separately. Those policies then provide informed initialization for multi-agent coordination, reducing the difficulty of joint training from scratch.

Lesson 5 — CTDE can coordinate multiple flexible assets without requiring the centralized critic during online execution

Centralized information is useful during training, while decentralized actors can later operate with local observations. This is especially attractive when many DER controllers must act quickly.

Lesson 6 — a TVPP is more than a market aggregator when network feasibility is included

The paper emphasizes the technical VPP concept: profitable market participation must remain compatible with voltage, line, and nodal constraints inside the distribution network.

14. Limitations / what remains unsolved

A. Future work explicitly stated by the authors

The paper identifies the following extensions:

  • additional flexibility products, especially frequency regulation;
  • more detailed physical models of other flexible demand, such as thermostatically controlled loads;
  • explicit economic models of user participation and incentives.

B. Further research space visible from the model

  • Forecast-to-decision uncertainty propagation: the CNN-LSTM produces quantile bounds, but the downstream RL/LP framework does not formulate an explicit chance-constrained, robust, or distributionally robust optimization problem based on those predictive distributions.
  • 5-minute data construction: the source data are described as 15-minute series “refined” to 5-minute resolution, but the paper does not clearly specify the resampling/interpolation procedure or quantify the uncertainty introduced by this transformation.
  • Reward engineering: many coefficients are manually tuned through sensitivity analysis. Policy performance may therefore depend materially on reward scaling and parameter tuning.
  • EV user economics: charging is offered for free and user satisfaction is represented mainly through departure SOC. Willingness to participate, compensation, inconvenience, and battery degradation are not explicitly priced.
  • Battery degradation: ESS and EV cycling costs are not explicitly modeled in the reported objective/reward structure.
  • Market-price uncertainty: predicted prices enter the RL states, but the paper does not formulate an explicit market-price uncertainty model or risk measure.
  • Real-world validation: results are simulation-based on IEEE 33-bus and historical datasets; no HIL or field deployment is reported.
